speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGENDA AND CANADIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked me yesterday whether I would have a word to say with reference to the commonwealth prime ministers' conference and the Canadian representation at that meeting. I would advise that I shall be leaving this afternoon and, as already announced, I shall visit Belfast on the way at the invitation of the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. On the 5th and 6th of March I shall be in Dublin as a guest of the Irish government for discussions with the Prime Minister of Ireland, Mr. Lemass.
I can assure hon. members that I shall take with me the warm wishes of this house and of Canadians generally, and I shall pay tribute to those of Irish blood who have made so great a contribution to Canada.
Sir, in regard to the prime ministers' meeting, it will commence, as hon. members know, on March 8 and continue until March 16. I shall be accompanied by the Secretary of State, and next week the Minister of Justice will also proceed to London in connection with the meetings.
These meetings of prime ministers are indispensable in commonwealth affairs. They exemplify the process of consultation which lies at the heart of the commonwealth relationship. They represent and are a recurrent symbol of the partnership and diversity of the commonwealth. They provide each national leader with an opportunity to understand the problems and the hopes of the other member nations.
As the Leader of the Opposition knows from personal experience, there is a candour in these meetings which ensures that they are profitable for all who participate. In the past 15 years since the war the commonwealth
has undergone a transformation in membership which has not only increased its usefulness and its opportunities in world affairs, but which has at the same time brought about new complexities and problems into the association.
This meeting of prime ministers will face problems of far-reaching significance, the most conspicuous of these being the continued membership of South Africa. I take it that in general the views of the parties in the house were set out in detail last March and April during the discussions that took place here. Since then the leader of the C.C.F. has given the views of his party. I take it that the Leader of the Opposition holds, because he has said nothing to the contrary, much the same views that he expressed during the debates nine or ten months ago. However, if there is any alteration in that viewpoint I would welcome hearing the hon. gentleman express his views in this regard at this time.
The essence of these meetings is that there shall be serious discussion without predetermined positions being taken. I can only express my conviction that the prime ministers will be inspired by a determination that in what they do the commonwealth will be preserved and strengthened and will be made an association even more effective as a vehicle of international partnership than ever before.
We sometimes fail to realize the tremendous diversity of opinion because of geography, size, culture, race and colour that is convened in these conferences. No one attending them can but have a greater knowledge of the problems faced everywhere in the world because of these diversities. Indeed I repeat what I have said on other occasions, that this body, transcending as it does the boundaries that ordinarily separate peoples of various races and colours, has a message for all mankind.
It is a practice in these meetings that the prime ministers should discuss the most urgent international issues of the day. I expect that there will be a very full review of the Congo situation and that in Laos, which are of concern to nations everywhere. Then there is the question of disarmament, which demands the attention of peoples everywhere. In this connection I shall naturally be bringing before the meeting the strong conviction of the Canadian government that there should be no relaxation- of the effort to achieve

Commonwealth Conference progress in disarmament, and will emphasize, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has done so effectively, that the middle and smaller nations have a definitive role to play in this process, a role which cannot be discharged by the greater powers by themselves.
There will be before the conference the question of the admission of Sierra Leone. There will be an application for membership from the republic of Cyprus. Beyond that I know the house would not expect me to go. However, immediately on my return I will report the progress made at the conference and, in general, outline and discuss the attitudes taken by the conference as a whole without, of course, revealing the discussions which in the interest of frankness are regarded as confidential.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGENDA AND CANADIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext:
I am sure all hon. members will have listened with great interest to the Prime Minister's statement on the forthcoming commonwealth prime ministers' conference. There is no doubt that in the long list of such conferences this will be one of the most important because the problems it will face are difficult and complex and will require all that flexibility of approach, wisdom and understanding which, I think it can be said, have been displayed at prime ministers' meetings in the past.
It was intriguing to me, Mr. Speaker, to read in the London Times this morning a dispatch from its diplomatic correspondent which I think should be given all the authority usually attached to such dispatches, giving the agenda of the forthcoming meeting, not in exact terms but as subjects which would be discussed. It was interesting to learn from that dispatch-and I am sure the Prime Minister's words this morning confirm it-that among the most important subjects of discussion will be disarmament so that if possible the commonwealth, can, at discussions at the United Nations, present a united front on this subject. Particular reference was made to the atomic test ban. In addition, the limitation of membership in the nuclear club is something the commonwealth prime ministers should discuss, especially in view of the fact that when a resolution on this subject was introduced at the United Nations by the Irish delegation last December the commonwealth delegations were badly split, Canada joining, I believe, with some of the Asian and African members in accepting that resolution limiting the nuclear club to countries now in possession of that weapon, while other members of the commonwealth abstained on it. This is one of the things in respect of which the commonwealth could bring about at least a greater measure of unity in its members.

According to the Times correspondent there will also be up for consideration the admission of communist China to the United Nations. Indeed, I am sure that the whole future of the United Nations will be discussed in London again to see if the commonwealth can present a united front in constructive proposals that will strengthen our world organization.
Our Prime Minister has mentioned the question of membership in the commonwealth. I have no doubt, of course, that this will be not only among the most important but also among the most difficult subjects up for consideration in view of the necessity of agreement being reached within this conference in regard to new members; or in regard to a member which has changed its status to a republic, seeking membership in the commonwealth. I, of course, refer in the last category to South Africa.
The position of the official opposition in regard to race discrimination and the policy of apartheid as practised in South Africa remains as described by myself in this house when this matter was discussed previously. I have no doubt that the effect of policies of racial and other forms of discrimination on membership in the commonwealth will have to be discussed at this meeting. I do not propose to go any further than that at this time.
The admission of Cyprus is another problem which the Prime Minister has mentioned. It is interesting and encouraging to realize that not very long ago many of the people of Cyprus were in arms against the United Kingdom. At this conference, after a tremendous majority in the legislature, Cyprus will be asking for admission to the commonwealth, and it may well be that Archbishop Makarios himself may turn up at a meeting of commonwealth leaders. Nothing could better express the flexibility, vitality and enduring strength of our commonwealth than that kind of situation.
The problems of increased membership in the commonwealth, however, are also complex. Perhaps at this meeting some consideration will have to be given to the question of whether institutional arrangements are now required in a commonwealth which is growing so fast and which will soon comprise 16, 18 or 20 members of varying degrees of size, strength and responsibility.
I have no doubt that the prime ministers will be devoting all the attention they can and bringing to bear all the wisdom and energies they possess to the question of commonwealth action in the direction of increasing the strength, co-operation and unity of this association in the search for international peace and security; and that they will do

everything they can to ensure the freedom, without discrimination of any kind, of all peoples within the boundaries of the member nations.
In so far as any progress can be made in that direction-and I am sure our own Prime Minister will do what he can to contribute to that progress-the conference and the Prime Minister will, I know, receive the support of all Canadians, as he will certainly receive and deserve the good wishes of the official opposition.
We wish the Prime Minister a pleasant journey. It is starting off well in that he is going to visit Ireland first. Perhaps he will be able to do something to help realize the vision of a united Ireland. Perhaps also he will visit Blarney castle. We wish the Prime Minister a pleasant journey and a most useful sojourn in London, and a safe return to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the prime ministers' commonwealth conference will be discussing many important questions. One of the most important in my opinion will be the economic well-being of member nations of the commonwealth. This will mean a discussion of trade and ways and means of expanding trade, and I would hope as well a discussion of a more far-reaching program to provide economic assistance to the underdeveloped nations in the commonwealth.
Canada should take a lead in this field. I suggest that in recent months there have been indications that Canada is falling back in this role. Instead of increasing, our economic assistance is decreasing at this time. I would hope-

subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGENDA AND CANADIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext: On a point of order, this is an inaccurate statement and really should not be made. No doubt the hon. member Tead it in some newspaper article, but the statement is not correct.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGENDA AND CANADIAN PERSONNEL

A further supplementary estimate will have to be brought down to make it an inaccurate statement. I hope the government will take action to show that the minister's statement is correct. There is certainly room for a vast expansion in economic assistance, and whether we are falling slightly behind or going slightly ahead I suggest the Canadian people feel that the government should be taking an active lead in this field.
Second, I suggest that in international affairs the government should continue a firm stand in opposing any expansion of the nuclear club. It would be a great mistake for more nations to have nuclear weapons. I would hope also that the commonwealth would take a firm stand in opposition to further nuclear tests. At this time, when there are
Columbia River Power Development reports that France is considering a fourth nuclear explosion, I would hope that this subject would be on the agenda for discussion by the commonwealth prime ministers, and that the weight of the commonwealth should be in opposition to further nuclear tests.
The Prime Minister has made special reference to the South African situation. I think the position of this group is rather clear. We have been and are very much opposed to discrimination in any form. We feel that Canada should speak out and the Prime Minister should speak out for Canadians in expressing that opposition. South Africa has had a vote and has decided to become a republic. She will perhaps be asking for admission to the commonwealth as a republic. I suggest that it should be made clear to South Africa that her policies must be changed before sympathetic consideration can be given to bringing her into the commonwealth of nations. I suggest that such an attitude and such a policy would increase the chances of discrimination in this nation being reduced.
We all wish the Prime Minister a successful journey. We hope the conference will be successful, and we shall be looking forward to the report he makes to parliament on his return.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGENDA AND CANADIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext:
May I be allowed to say to the Leader of the Opposition how very deeply I appreciate his gracious words, and may I express my thanks to the leader of the C.C.F. for his good wishes.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the constitutional developments that are taking place. This question is one that will naturally exercise the minds and thoughts of those in attendance. As he pointed out, membership in the commonwealth is increasing so rapidly that it may in effect deny that intimacy and closeness of relationship in discussion which has been characteristic of the past. At what point do you or do you not draw the line? Shall a member nation have a given population or more? These are problems that face the commonwealth. In the light of the developments that are taking place, the commonwealth will have to decide whether it would not be appropriate for the meetings, while held generally in the centre of the commonwealth, might, not on a rotational basis but from time to time, take place in other capitals of the commonwealth.
Again I express my thanks to the Leader of the Opposition and to the leader of the C.C.F.

speechtext:
should like to make a statement with regard

Columbia River Power Development to the Columbia river treaty, and with particular reference to the report of the British Columbia energy board. I do so in response to requests from many members, including in particular the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, as well as in response to the request which was made yesterday.
The government has now secured the text of interim report No. 1 of the British Columbia energy board, and has had an opportunity to analyse it. I can say at once that there is no point raised in the report that did not receive exhaustive consideration in the course of Canada-British Columbia discussions and in the course of the negotiation of the treaty. I should like also to emphasize that the British Columbia government were directly represented and participated fully at every stage of these discussions and negotiations. They participated fully in the working out of all provisions, and accepted every section and word of the treaty. Their engineers and technical advisers, including two of the members of the British Columbia energy board, participated fully in the determination of all figures and estimates on the basis of which the treaty was recommended. The British Columbia government accepted the conclusions reflected in the treaty on every one of the points now raised by the British Columbia energy board's report.
The energy board's report suggests that the treaty should not be ratified "without prior consideration" of certain factors. The essential point I want to make is that all these factors have received exhaustive prior consideration over a period of 17 years. Among other things the board suggests that discussions "have not yet proceeded to a point where any precise estimate can be obtained of the actual nature and quantity of power which will reach the B.C. load centres". This is a quotation from the board's report. A reference to the treaty and the annexes will show that the utmost precision possible at this stage has been introduced for the determination of precisely these matters at the only time they can be determined with complete certainty, when the treaty is in effect and operation has begun.
These are the kinds of matter that can only be determined finally when actual operation commences. To suggest that ratification and thus commencement of construction be delayed until a precise determination is obtained on all these points would mean therefore that nothing would ever start. The advance information and estimates on the Columbia project are at least as full and detailed as those available at the stage when other major programs were committed for construction; for instance, the St. Lawrence seaway.


In general, the British Columbia energy board's report asks that everything be determined precisely in advance, whereas in the nature of this kind of development some things can only be finally determined at a later stage. The treaty provides especially rigorous principles and procedures for making this determination.
The British Columbia energy board's report also seems to suggest that storage projects should only be brought in at the theoretically ideal time. This might be an engineer's dream, but it is simply not possible to ensure in a negotiated arrangement of this magnitude where commitments and plans have necessarily to be made far in advance. The British Columbia government is well aware of the reasons for the timetable for the Canadian projects included in the treaty. They know that any difference sequence or timetable would detract from the great value secured for all these Canadian projects.
What matters now is what the British Columbia government intends to do about this report. The real question is whether or not British Columbia and Canada are going ahead with the Columbia development. If it is to go ahead, ratification must take place without any unnecessary delay, and a start on the projects must be made just as soon as possible. Surely nothing should be allowed to jeopardize not only the power benefits but also the many millions of man hours of employment and the general economic stimulus waiting to be realized through the treaty project. If the British Columbia government is going to impose further delay on the basis of some of the points that have been raised again by the board's report, there is grave danger that this will imperil the treaty and the entire Columbia river development, not only for this year but perhaps forever.
The United States Senate will commence its consideration of this treaty as early as March 8. Let there be no doubt that the government of Canada stands ready to proceed with ratification at once.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has made what I think is a very important statement on this matter. We on this side were of the impression, having regard to what the Prime Minister said some weeks ago, that consideration of this treaty by this house and by the committee to which it would presumably be submitted, and action by this parliament, would not be taken until suitable arrangements had been made with the provincial government concerned.

Having said that, I should add that yesterday in reply to a question I put the Prime Minister did say that no decision had yet been taken as to whether the agreement would be brought forward before the event to which the hon. gentleman made reference.
Now, Mr. Speaker, of course the negotiation and ratification of treaties is the responsibility of the federal government. Although in accordance with a convention of our constitution treaties are submitted to parliament for consideration and approval, once a treaty is ratified, the federal government has an international obligation in respect of that treaty vis-a-vis the other signatory country or countries. While that is true of the implementation of the treaty, nevertheless in so far as that implementation deals with matters under provincial jurisdiction it is the responsibility also of the provincial government concerned. If we proceeded in this house with consideration of this treaty, and with action in regard to it, before those matters had been concluded with the provincial government which are essential to the implementation of the treaty, we might find ourselves in very grave difficulties indeed. I do not want to be dogmatic or final about the matter, but I do want to point out one of the implications in the minister's statement, as I understood it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for drawing to my attention the implication he has taken, because I do think this should be cleared up. My statement is a statement of the position of the Canadian government; that is that the Canadian government has confidence the treaty represents the best advantage to Canada, and stands ready to proceed with ratification. This statement is quite consistent with what the Prime Minister said because, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, it is important to know exactly what the position of British Columbia is and that, of course, will have to be determined before a final decision is made by the government of Canada. My statement is a statement of the position of the Canadian government, a position about which there should be no doubt. We stand ready to ratify this treaty at the earliest possible moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to announce the promulgation of revised Canada mining regulations which apply to the Northwest Territories and certain other federal lands.
The regulations for the disposition of mining rights in the Northwest Territories and on other federal lands outside the provinces and the Yukon have been completely revised and modernized. Formerly known as the quartz mining regulations, they had not been basically revised since the early thirties. In the interim, changes have taken place in exploration and production techniques and in other facets of the industry which required recognition in new regulations.
About two years ago my department began a basic revision of this mineral disposition law. Wide consultation was held with industry while the revisions were being studied. Public meetings were held on two occasions in Yellowknife, Edmonton and Toronto, with large numbers of the mining fraternity attending. Three separate sets of drafts were distributed for comment and over one hundred briefs were received from associations, companies and individuals. This active co-operation from industry has been of great help to us in drawing up suitable regulations.
The revised regulations rest on two principles; first, to encourage exploration, development and production, and second, to protect

Revised Mining Regulations the interest of the people of Canada in the valuable resources which are administered under these regulations.
I would like to outline a few of the main changes brought about by the new regulations. There are, of course, a great many other revisions in the regulations which are of a technical or administrative nature which I will not mention at this time.
It is the policy of this government to ensure that Canadians have an opportunity to participate in the ownership and development of our resources. This policy is made effective in these regulations by providing for Canadian participation requirements at the lease stage, just as in the Canada oil and gas regulations. A lease to hold or produce minerals will only be issued to Canadian citizens or corporations incorporated in Canada in which at least 50 per cent of the issued shares are owned by Canadians, or whose shares are listed on a Canadian stock exchange, and in whose financing and ownership Canadians have an opportunity to participate.
The maximum claim tenure period for new claims is set at ten years to avoid the problems inherent in long claim tenure without activity. If the ground is to be held beyond ten years, claims must be converted into leases and, as I have said, leasing is mandatory whenever production starts. Leases are for a 21 year period with a privilege of renewal, and lease rentals may be offset by exploratory work.
In place of the rather unwieldy reservation system in our former regulations, we have introduced a prospecting permit system. These permits are for a maximum three year period and require minimum fixed exploratory expenditures each year, guaranteed by deposits. There will be no special arrangements with individual companies or payments or rentals to the crown. They will be issued on a "first come, first served" basis and only in the winter season, in order that everyone may know the areas granted well before the beginning of the prospecting season.
A large area around Great Slave lake where prospecting is active will be exempted from issuance of permits and, in fact, permits will not be issued in any areas which are being actively explored. They are designed for the more remote areas which have not been actively explored and where exploration over a larger spread of acreage for a short time, using modern methods, is justified. It is confidently expected that this permit system will encourage exploration in remote areas.
Areas not actively under permit will, of course, be open to normal staking and in no event can more than 12 per cent of the permit area be retained in claims by the permit holder.

The new regulations contain transitional clauses framed with the utmost care to protect and confirm rights given under former regulations, to assure that they are not abrogated.
There are a great many other changes which will cut red tape and reduce costs to the prospector and developer.
I am confident that the new Canada mining regulations will provide a sound basis for investment in the exploration and production of federal mineral resources, and will also protect the rights of the Canadian public, the owners of these resources, in line with the government's policy of northern development. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, that very important statement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) will certainly please the whole population of the Northwest Territories.
However, before being in a position to commit ourselves definitely on the contents of those amendments to the act, I think it would be wise to consider them in fuller detail.
I wish to congratulate the minister for that initiative, and to assure him that the measure will indeed be welcomed by the people concerned.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE TO UNIVERSITY OF MALAYA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make an announcement concerning a new type of Colombo plan assistance which has been arranged with Malaya and Singapore. At the request of the government of the federation of Malaya and of the government of the state of Singapore, the government of Canada has approved a project whereby the University of British Columbia will establish and develop, in the Kuala Lumpur and Singapore divisions of the University of Malaya, courses in accounting and business administration. The University of British Columbia will also undertake the necessary research in business and industry in the federation of Malaya and in the state of Singapore with a view to adapting these research findings for teaching purposes.
This is the first occasion when a Canadian university has undertaken a program of technical assistance as the agent of the government of Canada. The project, subject to annual review, will continue over a period of five years, and will involve sending out to Malaya and Singapore members of the faculty of the University of British Columbia for research and teaching duties.

When the program is well launched in the two universities abroad, it is proposed to bring to Canada selected students from the universities at Kuala Lumpur and at Singapore for training at the University of British Columbia and elsewhere in Canada. Upon completion of their training these students will return home to replace successively the teaching and research staff of the University of British Columbia in the University of Malaya. When this program is in full progress there will be six faculty members of the University of British Columbia at the Kuala Lumpur and Singapore divisions of the University of Malaya, and six students from the University of Malaya who will be pursuing their studies in Canada.
The costs of this program, including salaries of the professors of the University of British Columbia abroad, the training of these students from Malaya and Singapore in Canada, travel, and the necessary equipment including library books, business machines and other supplies, will be met from funds voted to finance Canada's participation in the Colombo plan.
It is thought that this project undertaken by the University of British Columbia on behalf of the government of Canada may be the first of a series of such arrangements whereby a Canadian university or other institution would undertake a specific program of technical assistance on behalf of the Canadian government. There are obvious advantages in concentrating Canada's aid programs upon specific and demonstrable needs abroad-there is a great lack of accountants and business administrators in Malaya and in Singapore-and it is clearly an efficient procedure to entrust such a project to a university in Canada well equipped to plan and carry it out with its own specialized research and teaching staff.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be received by the house and the country, I am sure, with great interest. It is noteworthy that the minister should have made this statement today in view of the interest that was shown yesterday by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) when he suggested that consideration might be given to emulat-ting the plan now being established in the United States in establishing a peace corps in undeveloped lands.
This, of course, is not precisely the same concept, but it has many similar features. The arrangements made for assistance to Singapore and the federation of Malaya as announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs continue arrangements that
Colombo Plan
were first established, I think, in 1956. It is important that this aid to these two states, Singapore and the federation of Malaya, should be of a generous character because of the need for assistance.
It is interesting that the great University of British Columbia, on the Pacific coast, should be the first university to participate in this interesting and, I am sure, useful venture. It must have been a matter of great pride to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, coming as he does from Vancouver and British Columbia, to make this announcement in so far as the University of British Columbia's participation is concerned.
However, the minister will not mind my saying to him, as one University of Toronto man to another, that it is to be hoped that in the pursuit of this plan that university, as well as the university in Windsor, Assumption University, and other universities in Canada, which are devoted to Asian studies, will be given an opportunity to contribute at some future date.
In this particular one should not forget that the first Asian study department to be set up in Canada was at McGill, under Professor Smith. If anyone doubts the catholicity of my university interests, this statement will clearly remove that doubt.

Mr. Speaker, may I say that we all understand the envy and jealousy of the hon. member for Essex East. However, may I say that we in British Columbia take a different attitude from the hon. member. Anything from Canada is good and we are proud of it, irrespective of the province or the university participating. However, you will of course understand the great interest with which I listened to the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because I also come from Vancouver and British Columbia. We are exceedingly proud, of course, that there has been an arrangement made on this most important matter of assistance to other states and countries whereby the University of British Columbia is able to be of help.
I am in particular very happy about the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs because, although I take no credit for it, it is in line with a speech I made in this house during the last session as a result of information given to me in Singapore and Malaya on the occasion of the visit of the official Canadian delegation to those countries. It was impressed upon us by the people of Singapore and Malaya, Indonesia, Thailand, Iran and other countries that they felt the greatest help Canada could give would be to have our technicians and university people go to their countries, understand them, help them in their countries in

Colombo Plan
educational, administrative and business methods, and then have, on the basis of that understanding and knowledge, the acceptance of students from those countries into our own universities.
I have nothing but the highest commendation for the initiation of this policy whereby Canadian universities first send people to these countries to understand and assist them, and then follow up with their students coming to our country. We are, of course, very happy about the announcement of this policy and, being human, we are very proud that the first university in this field is U.B.C. We hope to see, and we have every hope that this will be so, the policy extended and that the university about which the hon. member for Essex East is so concerned will have an opportunity to learn from the experience of U.B.C.

Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production): Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce to the house the plans of Polymer Corporation Limited for a new plant at Sarnia for the production of polybutadiene. Construction will commence during the summer of 1961, with a view to being in production before the end of 1962.
This plant is estimated to cost between $8 million and $10 million and will be the first commercial unit in Canada for the production of stereo-specific rubbers, a new family of rubbers made possible by advances in special catalysts developed in the last eight years. These rubbers are of particular interest in heavy duty truck and bus tires. Polymer has already been producing substantial quantities of polybutadiene in its plant located in Sarnia. Large quantities have been used for factory evaluation.

This is the second unit of the expansion program for Polymer which I announced last fall, and emphasizes the continuing growth and diversification of the company's facilities in Sarnia.

He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house. It has just been said that I was so hesitant about this motion that I sat down after reading it out. I sat down so that Your Honour would have a chance to read the motion, and in order that the Prime Minister and the leader of the C.C.F. party might have a copy of it. If I did not resume my statement immediately it was through courtesy to the Speaker, to the Prime Minister and to the leader of the other party, not through hesitancy. In doing so I followed the normal practice of this house for years.
The Prime Minister has already indicated that he does not consider this matter to be one of urgency. There can be no question, of course, about its importance. It deals with a concrete proposal which has at last been

advanced by the government in order to alleviate unemployment. But this proposal, as we have understood and studied it, is in such uncertain terms that it is already causing uncertainty and uneasiness in the country with regard to its application. Surely, therefore, it is necessary to clear up at once the nature of this proposal, the manner of its operation and the effect it will have on the economy.
We did our best last evening to have a discussion on this matter but it was ruled by the Chair to be out of order. I am not complaining about that, but there was no possibility of our continuing the discussion of it on the budget resolutions before the house which, according to the Minister of Finance, had nothing whatever to do with this matter. Therefore we had to find some other way of discussing the subject at once.
When the house rose last night my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who asked what the business was to be for the next day, suggested that perhaps we could discuss this matter today on the estimates of the Department of Labour; or, if that was not possible-and the leader of the house said it was not possible-possibly we could discuss it on Monday on a supply motion. That has not been found possible, either-and I am not complaining about that-but in view of the immediate urgency of getting this question cleared up so the country may know what these regulations mean and how they can be applied at once to the unemployment situation, surely it is not necessary to wait until some time next week when the government brings forward the estimates of the Department of Labour.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It seems to me Your Honour has to make a ruling which is difficult because of its qualitative nature. Because of that, it seems to me that what you really want is an honest opinion as to the question of urgent public importance. I can only say for the C.C.F. party that we have been stunned by the haziness and inadequacy of the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Labour. Speaking for my constituents and my party I certainly feel this is urgently important. We know something about the criteria mentioned in this motion, and for this reason we would urge Your Honour to allow it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of urgency I think you have to take into account that a request such as this asks the house to set aside the business arranged for the day in question. Now, the business which it is intended to bring before the house today is consideration of the estimates

of the Department of Agriculture, and I do not think anyone would wish to argue that this does not constitute urgent and essential business to be considered by this house because of the economic factors which will be determined by the acceptance or otherwise of the government's program for agriculture for the year.
The second point to be considered is this. This question was discussed last night. In our opinion the hon. member for Essex East was out of order, but we permitted him to go ahead without interruption for a full 30 minutes discussing this particular subject. We could easily have interrupted the hon. member and asked him to refrain from comment but we did not do so, and so the matter was considered by the house last night. The hon. member for Port Arthur similarly without interruption followed on the same subject for about 15 minutes. Therefore we have heard the views of the opposition with regard to this important problem.
Hon. members on the opposition side asked that this matter be taken up on Monday and Tuesday. Consequently they were of the opinion last night that it was not of such urgency that it had to be discussed today. It so happens that Monday, under our rules, is a private members' day and is so set out. We are consequently going ahead with that.
Finally, the Prime Minister has pointed out that the estimates of the Department of Labour will be up for consideration next week. They will be called, and I think I can safely give the assurance now that they will come before the house on Thursday, which will give ample opportunity for full debate on this particular problem on Thursday and on Friday if necessary. Hon. members of the opposition were prepared to discuss this question on Monday and Tuesday of next week, so it is only a matter of our making the suggestion that these matters be discussed on Thursday.
I would conclude by saying that I think it would be wrong to interrupt the business of the day to discuss this particular problem when there will be an early opportunity to debate it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the practice that has been established in the house is, I think, clearly set out, as Your Honour knows, in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100. Before Your Honour entertains a motion of this character he must be assured that there are four elements present.
The first is that the matter is one of the administrative responsibility of the government, and I believe there is no doubt about that.

The next is that it is a matter of definite, urgent public importance, and I think that has been admitted by the statement which the Prime Minister has made.
The third and perhaps the most important element of them all is that of the urgency of debate upon which Your Honour, generally speaking, seeks advice from both sides of the house. It is to this point that the house leader addressed himself, namely that it would not be wise in his opinion and that of the government to adjourn the business of the house which is going to be under consideration shortly to discuss this matter.
That reference to urgency of debate is the basis upon which we on this side of the house differ completely from the house leader. The reasons are that when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit of the subject matter being brought up early enough, then there is urgency of debate. It is all right for the Prime Minister and the house leader to say that the estimates of the Department of Labour will be called, but for the last two weeks we have been asking that these estimates be called and have received no satisfactory reply to that request. If our request had been complied with earlier perhaps there would have been an opportunity of discussing some of these matters, but we were not given that opportunity.
Another thing we ask is that we be given the opportunity of discussing the matter on an amendment to the motion to go into supply. We are told that Monday is a private members' day and that therefore we cannot discuss this matter on Monday. Why should we have to wait until Thursday, when even then we do not know whether some other matter of importance will come to the attention of the government and it may decide then not to call the estimates of the Department of Labour.
It is not the statement by the house leader that this will be done on Thursday that determines the urgency of the debate. It is the question which is before the house, namely the statement made by the Minister of Labour yesterday. It is no answer for the house leader and those who sit on the other side of the house to say that we had an opportunity of discussing this last night. That is not so. There was no opportunity of discussing this last night-

I have read the debate very carefully and there is no doubt in my mind, I say with respect to the Prime Minister, that there was not last night an opportunity of discussion afforded within the meaning of the words "urgency of debate" as is meant under the rules.
The fourth criteria that determines this matter is that of opportunity. There will be no opportunity to deal with this matter before Thursday at the earliest, if one accepts the statement made by the house leader. In view of the importance of this question and in view of the uneasiness and anxiety in the country because of the application of this criteria, I submit with deference that we should now be given the opportunity we seek and that the motion should be accepted so that we may discuss these matters of urgent public importance.

I shall be glad to hear from the hon. member on this point if he thinks it is necessary after I have concluded. One difficulty-and it is one to which the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) could perhaps address himself-is the possibility that if the motion is permitted it might anticipate a matter which has been previously appointed for consideration by the house. I do not see that this matter has been appointed for consideration.
The subject matter of the request, namely "the inadequate and restrictive character of the criteria to be used as the basis of the designation of depressed areas" arises out of the statement of policy made yesterday by the Minister of Labour, which is found at page 2569 of Hansard. I take it that it was purely a statement of government policy, an administrative decision, and I do not see that it necessarily comes before the house for debate under any of the orders now on the order paper. It is true that it might be discussed on the labour estimates.
With respect to the suggestion that it could have been or was discussed last night, I do not accept that proposition because it is agreed that if it had been discussed last night the discussion would have been out of order, and I do not think opportunity for debate which would be out of order can be considered opportunity for debate.

The matter having arisen yesterday and it being a matter of national significance and importance, it seems to me that as far as I have gone with the assistance which I have had from hon. members, and for which I thank them, if this is not a matter which has been appointed for debate so that we would be anticipating a debate which will necessarily occur in the course of this session, I might very well accept the proposition.
If the hon. member for Essex East wishes to say anything on that point or if any other hon. member can assist me on that point, I would be glad to hear him now.

Therefore I feel I must put the request before the house in the terms of standing order 26, and so that all hon. members will understand it I shall read it in so far as it has not yet been read. Subsection 3 of section 26 reads:
-Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house. If objection is taken, Mr. Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and, if more than 20 members rise accordingly, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I just ask a question with regard to your earlier remarks, sir? I understood you to say that this matter has not been appointed for discussion in the house, but surely it is not the practice of the house to provide immediately an opportunity for a discussion of matters of urgent public importance. The statement of the Minister of Labour was made just yesterday afternoon, and it is not normal for the government, following a statement, to immediately name the period at which that statement may be taken up for debate. I think it is rather pressing things a little far and will establish a difficult precedent if, whenever an announcement of government policy is made in this house, someone from the government side must state when it will be available for debate.
I might draw your attention to the fact that this morning we had, I think, five statements, some of which concern government policy. Am I now obliged to name the date on which those will be taken up for debate? These concern the Department of External

Affairs, the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. They are all important matters, and it would be extraordinarily awkward to have to immediately name the date and the hour when those matters would come up for consideration.
I suggest that we are in the same position here. The Minister of Labour made a statement yesterday declaring government policy, and I have now suggested that the opportunity for debating it will occur early next week. I doubt very much whether I should be called upon to do more than that. I think you could argue urgency of debate with regard to the other matters that were announced as government policy this morning, and we might then continue day after day, at the wish of the opposition debating those matters. Yet in the ordinary course of the organization of business there is always ample opportunity to debate important matters in the house. In this particular instance it is only a deferment of, say, 48 hours beyond what the opposition suggested as the time for debate. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that further consideration might be given to this particular problem.

But what I want to draw to your attention, sir, are two statements in particular which are to be found in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, at page 91. Paragraph 8 reads:
Standing order 10 of the United Kingdom house, in force since 1882, also provides that a member may propose the adjournment of the house "for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance".

[Mr. Speaker.)
by the areas themselves at a time when there is unemployment, it seems to me I must accept the view that this is urgent.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion we have made to adjourn the house was put forward for the purpose of dealing with a matter which is, we think, not only of very great importance but also of immediate urgency because it deals with a proposal put

Labour Conditions
forward by the government in the hope that it will alleviate the unemployment situation in certain areas. We all know the seriousness of that situation generally, but it is of particular seriousness in particular areas. Presumably, to deal with that aspect of the situation, the government brought forward yesterday certain regulations laying down criteria to be used-and I am quoting from the motion-as a basis for the designation of areas eligible for double depreciation under the proposals of the budget of December 20.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) introduced these resolutions yesterday he stated that these areas eligible for double depreciation under that program would be areas where there had been a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget statement of December 20 referred to those areas as areas of chronic unemployment. The budget about which the Minister of Finance was speaking when he made that statement was that which included the policy referred to by the Minister of Labour yesterday in announcing these regulations and putting forward these proposals.
We think it is quite reasonable to refer to those areas not only as areas of chronic unemployment, as the government has done, but as depressed areas. An area of chronic unemployment within the meaning of the terms used by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance is, in our view, a depressed area. We do not see why there should be any squeamishness attached to the use of this expression. It is a word commonly used to characterize certain unfortunate areas. It has been used in the hearings before the Senate committee on manpower and unemployment. Indeed, it was used in the statement made before that committee by Professor Judek of the University of Ottawa on February 2. Professor Judek is no doubt well known to the Minister of Labour and, in fact, I believe his services have been used by the Department of Labour. In his own report to that committee the professor uses as a heading to one of his subparagraphs the phrase "full employment and depressed areas". So we think it is not improper to use that expression.
But it is not the expression itself that matters or how we designate these areas; it is what we are going to do in order to take them out of this condition of employment depression. For that purpose the government, at long last, yesterday produced some regulations. The purpose of these regulations and the policy behind them were announced as far back as December 20, 1960 when the Minister of Finance in that statement to
which I have already referred had this to say as reported on page 1007 of Hansard:
As a powerful Incentive-
I say at once that we do not think these regulations constitute a very powerful incentive. But the minister said:
As a powerful incentive to these ends-
The ends mentioned were the encouragement of initiative and enterprise and employment.
-X am pleased to announce measures to fulfil three major purposes: first, to assist new industries in areas where there is a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years; second, to aid the development of new products from processing operations not hitherto carried on in Canada; and, third, to encourage the production of new types of goods. Double depreciation will, at the option of the taxpayer, be allowed in respect of capital expenditures incurred in the first year for these purposes but may be applied in any of the first three years.
Then the hon. gentleman went on, and these are the words I have already referred to:
In some areas changing economic conditions have created a degree of chronic unemployment which requires special action.
Presumably the regulations introduced into the house yesterday by the Minister of Labour are designed to constitute that special action. It may be special, but it is not likely to be effective in the light of the problem with which it is meant to deal. Furthermore, at any time since December 20, or indeed before that date, this action could have been taken by the government. I know that the Minister of Finance, when we urged the designation of these areas and when we urged that action of this kind should be taken, replied by saying: we have to deal with the budget resolutions first. He abandoned that position last evening when he said as reported on page 2611 of Hansard:
-the matter is one for executive action within the terms of the existing legislation.
If that means anything at all it means that this kind of action could have been taken as executive action at any time since December 20 last by the government. If the government on December 20 or even previously, had an appreciation of the seriousness of the situation, as we on this side have had, surely it would have taken that action before now.
We did our best at that time to prod the government into action. We asked question after question as to when these areas were to be designated, how they were to be designated and which minister was to be responsible for implementing the policy in the statement of the Minister of Finance on December 20.

We asked if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) was to be responsible and we could not get an answer. We asked if the Minister of Labour was to be responsible and we could not get an answer. We then asked if the Minister of Finance was to be responsible and we could not get an answer. I think it was on Tuesday of this week when we asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and that hon. gentleman said, finally, that the Minister of Labour would be responsible for this matter and yesterday the regulations themselves were introduced and put on Hansard by the minister.
This kind of laboured, indecisive and late action is in startling contrast to that which has been taken quickly, decisively and effectively in Washington by the new president of the United States. This could have been done by the government at any time within the last three years. It was done in Washington within a few weeks of the accession to office of the new president who almost at once submitted to congress a measure not only dealing with general principles of assistance to depressed areas but designating 99 areas of the United States as depressed areas, taking the responsibility for them and asking congress to deal with them in legislative terms.
That is how action could have been taken in this country under existing legislation at any time since this serious unemployment problem confronted us. However, yesterday we did get the regulations. It is our contention that the regulations as they were put forward by the minister are inadequate and indefinite. To the extent that we can understand them they seem in some cases to be entirely unworkable and they are, in the light of the problem that faces the needy areas, surely quite unsatisfactory. They apply double depreciation to the specified areas established by the criteria laid down, but double depreciation is to be applied for one year and one year only. That year is to begin from any one of the first three years when the industry moves in.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what kind of incentive is that for an industry to move into an area which is already depressed? The government proposes to extend double depreciation for one year only. But the regulations as we have them before us are not likely to accomplish the purpose that I know the minister has in mind in putting them forward. They appear in dramatic contrast to the stand that this party has taken more than once in the last three years that this weapon of tax depreciation, if it is to be used against unemployment, should be used vigorously, quickly and decisively and that its application 90205-6-1674
Labour Conditions
should be more comprehensive than is indicated in the proposal introduced yesterday and now before us.
Before leaving the regulations themselves let me say that we expect during the course of the afternoon to hear from the Minister of Labour what the regulations actually mean in terms of application. We hope that the hon. gentleman will be able to clear up some of these difficulties of uncertainty that have already begun to make themselves felt throughout the country and to remove at least some of the disappointment that is being experienced concerning the inadequacy and ineffectiveness of these regulations.
Not only are the regulations inadequate but the procedure for their application to accomplish the purpose the government presumably has in mind is very difficult to understand and surely it represents a further abdication of responsibility by this government.
Who takes the initiative in this matter? Who starts the ball rolling, even this ball? It is not the federal government which does so, but the municipalities; they take the initiative. "Do it yourself," says the government to the municipalities. "If you feel you are a depressed area, tell us you think you are a depressed area and then we will see whether you fall under the criteria which we have laid down in the regulations. Ask us to investigate," says the government.
The government has this responsibility now. As I said a few moments ago, the government at any time in the last three years could have taken the initiative by order in council in accordance with the criteria which it has laid down in designating depressed areas and taking the necessary action to get them out of that category of depressed areas. The government has not done that. So far as we know, no order in council has been passed.
We pressed the Minister of Finance yesterday to find out whether any orders in council had already been passed under the income tax legislation which is now in effect. We have the right to deduce from the minister's silence that no action of any kind has been taken. We ask the minister now, how is action going to be taken under these regulations? Is there going to be a general order in council covering all applications which would simplify matters or is there to be required a separate order in council for every municipal request for assistance of this nature which has been found acceptable under these regulations?
We would like to get an answer from the government to that very important question and I am sure the municipalities would like

Labour Conditions
to know that at once. That is one of the reasons we have pressed for discussion of this matter this afternoon.
In explaining these regulations yesterday, as reported at page 2569 of Hansard, the Minister of Labour had this to say:
Hon. members of this house will recall that one objective of this program is to assist new industries in areas where there has been a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years.
We will find out in a minute what "over the years" means and how this will limit the applications of some of the areas of this country which need help most. The minister continued:
Areas which meet the following criteria may qualify under this program.
Presumably if an area does not meet these criteria it cannot qualify under this program. The minister then proceeded to set out the criteria. He said:
They are broken down into two categories; areas with a labour force of 10,000 and over, and areas with a labour force of less than 10,000. In those areas where the labour force is 10,000 and over the criteria are first, the area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category-
A surplus labour market category is a category that has already been established over the years by the Department of Labour and presumably that would be the category that would be used now. The minister continued:
-the area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category for 75 per cent or more of the 48 summer months-
Those are months when unemployment is lowest. I continue:
-from May to October, 1953-1960. Second, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-1960.
That is presumably over a period of eight summers.
Then, he went on:
Areas with a labour force of less than 10,000 must have been classified by the Department of Labour as in a surplus labour market category-
Again, we know what that means.
-for 50 per cent or more of the 48 summer months May to October, 1953-1960.
It is interesting to note the distinction made in these words. The words used are not:
Second, industrial employment conditions must have declined over the period 1953-1960.
That is what was stated to be necessary in the case of areas of 10,000 and over. The words used here are:
Second, industrial employment conditions must have generally deteriorated over the years.

Let me interpret in more specific terms and in accordance with the practice of the Department of Labour, Mr. Speaker, what these words apparently mean. First, the ratio of applications for employment on file with the national employment service to be paid workers including those looking for work must have exceeded 7 per cent for 24 or more summer months from May to October, 1953-1960. I ask the minister to inform the house how the Department of Labour is going to calculate that ratio in relation to areas below the 10,000 population? How is the Department of Labour going to do that? Is there any method now by which that can be done under the procedures already followed by the Department of Labour?
I call attention also to the fact-and it was mentioned last night by my hon. friend from Essex East-that the calculation is presumably to be made in relation to the applications for employment on file in the national employment service. This is a calculation that has been rejected by the government in relation to unemployment discussions in this house. They will have none of it. The bureau of statistics random sampling is to be the calculation accepted, and we in this house have accepted it as the basis of our discussion of unemployment and we use it as the statistical evidence of unemployment. But it is not used in these regulations. For some reason or other the government goes back to that calculation which it had rejected and uses now the applications for employment on file with the national employment service.
The second calculation is that industrial employment must have generally deteriorated over the years. I ask the minister once again what does he mean by that? How is that calculation to be applied to municipalities under 10,000 and then, again, in the areas of 10,000 or more? The principles enunciated by the minister seem to mean that the ratio of applications for employment on file with the national employment service to be paid workers including those looking for work must have exceeded, according to the Department of Labour, (a) 6 per cent in industrial areas of 25,000 or more for 36 or more months from May to October, 1953-60; or (b) 7 per cent in areas below 25,000 and above 10,000 for 36 or more months from May to October, 1953-60, and industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-1960.
Let us take the latter criterion first. To qualify for this kind of help, inadequate though it will be, in depressed areas as an incentive to getting new industries in those areas, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-60.

When the minister was putting these regulations forward yesterday he gave two examples of communities which in his opinion would qualify under the regulations. He mentioned Elliot Lake and Springhill, Nova Scotia. I should like him to explain to the house how under this criterion Elliot Lake could possibly qualify for this kind of assistance, although goodness knows no community in Canada, as an area of depressed conditions and unemployment, needs more assistance than Elliot Lake does at this time. Elliot Lake did not exist as a community in 1953, and yet to qualify for help Elliot Lake will have to prove that industrial employment declined during the period 1953-60. It is going to be very hard to prove decline from zero, because there was no employment in Elliot Lake in 1953.
I ask the minister how Springhill qualifies under these regulations when the disasters which have attacked Springhill in recent years began, not in 1953 but in 1956? I remember, also, Mr. Speaker, that in the application of this criterion the government has taken a period of eight summers. Four of those were good summers of high employment and prosperous conditions. They took four peak summers and four not so good. If they are to use the years after 1956, they have to qualify by averaging out the employment in those earlier years with the years of recession. I ask the minister how he is going to reconcile that kind of criterion with communities like Elliot Lake and Springhill?
These preliminary observations show how inadequate, how ineffective and how indecisive these regulations are. They have all the earmarks of something having been thrown together in a hurry because something had to be produced in this house. After three and half years of unemployment conditions and of recession, the government finally comes to this house and says, yes, we will do something about the depressed areas; we will do something by regulations that are now introduced this week, in March 1961. They are regulations which are entirely inadequate to meet the problem before us and which indeed are very difficult for any person to understand, let alone the municipalities which are given the responsibility of initiating action, a responsibility which should be that of this government.
