subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I was attempting to lead into a discussion of the responsibility of the government and the responsibility of the Department of Labour. Inasmuch as he is the minister, genial though he may be, who introduced this particular item yesterday, I felt it was necessary to relate the functions of the department and the minister's role in the cabinet to the cabinet as a whole. Over the past few years we have seen an increase in the role the Department of Labour is apparently playing in economic matters. This department was given increased authority and was supposed to be a new powerhouse in so far as the economy was concerned. The announcement made yesterday, I think, was an indication of the inability of the Department of Labour to meet this increased responsibility that has fallen upon its shoulders. I am of the opinion that there is practically no one in the department who is able to assess the effect of all the forces upon the economy and come up with any sensible approach to these problems. The announcement made yesterday in connection with this double depreciation factor is an indication of this.
The director of economics and research, I believe it is, of the Department of Labour, Mr. Dymond, appeared before the Senate committee on manpower and employment. He presented a well worded brief dealing with the economy of the nation. However, he made no conclusions, or no recommendations and the brief was not of an analytical

nature. Almost any grade 12 high school student could have written this type of brief about the economy.
The announcement concerning this double depreciation that will be allowed indicates also that we have a government that has a great love of the past but relatively little understanding of what might take place in the future. The setting of the period 1953-60 as the base period for determining whether or not an area will be eligible for double depreciation may be quite all right, but there is not one iota of sense in forgetting about the growth and expansion factors in the economy or those people who will be in the working force of our nation in 1961, 1962, 1963, and later years.
I feel that it is extremely unfortunate that the government has brought this matter forward in this form. It is extremely unfortunate for the areas that might be involved, and for the economy as a whole. It is an indication I believe of insufficient concern- I will not say lack of concern-or insufficient knowledge of the factors at play in the economy. It is an indication of insufficient concern for the welfare of the working force of the nation in those areas to which this double depreciation system may apply. The result of this provision will be to place those few areas in which it might apply in a sort of economic strait-jacket. I do not believe any straight statistical formula can be devised which would enable one to say: if you meet this test you may get some assistance; if you do not meet it, then you will not. I think it is unfair and discriminatory in that it seems to apply a mechanical and arbitrary test to depressed areas which did not become depressed areas as a result of any mechanical or arbitrary methods in the first place.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has dealt with the question of the government's selection of the months over the past eight years in which employment was high. I should like, then, only to mention it briefly in passing in order to emphasize that the months of June, July, August and September, the four months referred to, are the ones in which we have the lowest number of unemployed. What the minister is saying is that the government feels it will assist those areas which meet these tests that are based on a period when unemployment was the lowest, and it was only during the last four of those years that a high degree of unemployment actually emerged. With respect to some areas, the minister is saying that the four last years have to meet the test, and I think he is a little closer to the truth in that test because

those were the years during which this government was in office. I am not implying that the Liberals were any better.
In any event the minister is saying, in effect, that this proposal which purports to be a solution to the problem is repealed before it is enacted because it will not matter that much, the snap of a finger, in many places. As a matter of fact, the statistical requirement is coupled with a demand that there be a general decline in employment over the years. This assumption is entirely contrary to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said during the budget debate last year. He told us then that the problem of unemployment was solved. When we question them about unemployment, the answer which we regularly receive from this government, because they have not the intestinal courage to face up to the facts, is that the number of those employed has risen. We are told that there has been a regular increase in the number of people employed. If this is the case, then why tie these statistical criteria to a decline in employment in these particular areas? Either the hon. gentlemen were not being forthright in the years past and in the months past when they said there was an increase in the number employed-this was the answer to those who were accused of harping and carping about the number of unemployed-or else the indication in this plan that there must be a decline is not going to be an effective test at all.
In my opinion, this is just another mess of Tory garbage which means nothing. This announcement is designed to hoodwink the workers of this nation into thinking that this government has finally, after four years, come up with a solution to the problem of unemployment. Here is a government which has said over the past three or four years that there was no unemployment problem, but now it has finally come up with a solution to this problem. When the workers of this nation study the proposal, they will find there is nothing in it; it will prove to be just as empty as are the promises this government made before it got into office.
The only practical way in which this question of depressed or chronic unemployment areas can be dealt with is by making an assessment of the essential causes of the unemployment in these areas. This must be done before anything positive can take place. We must make a detailed examination to find out the original causes, because there are a variety of causes in different parts of the country. In one area the unemployment may result from one thing and in another it may
Labour Conditions
result from something else. There are a variety of factors responsible for this increasingly difficult situation.
The plan announced by the minister does not take into account the fact that unemployment is caused by different factors. His announcement suggests that Canada is equal in so far as concerns its chronic unemployment areas. Each area in Canada must meet the same set of circumstances before it can qualify for relief from its distressed condition. The government in its announcement has not taken into account any of these varying factors and the plan is only to be instituted for an interim period of time.
Has any thought been given to technological changes? Is this fact reflected in the statement made by the minister? Displaced workers who require new skills in order to secure employment have not been considered. Has any consideration been given to the decline of industry in certain areas? Is that something which should be taken into the picture? Some areas have experienced migration of industry because of a disappearance of resources, transportation difficulties and other similar changes. As reflected by the announcement of the minister, no account has been taken in this regard. Certainly there has been a depletion or exhaustion of certain natural resources in some areas, and this situation should be considered in order to arrive at equitable relief. Has any consideration been given to these various conditions as reflected in the minister's announcement? No, Mr. Speaker, no consideration has been given. Has the government considered the change in imports and exportations and the effect these changes have upon certain areas? This again is not reflected in the statement of the minister. Has any consideration been given by the government to the lay-offs that have taken place in the last year? No, this has not been taken into account. We have in this country certain areas that rely on the establishment of one industry, such as the oil industry, the steel industry, or in my own area of Kitimat. the aluminum industry. Has any account been taken of the situation that exists in this regard? No account has been taken of these factors at all. Has any consideration been given to population shifts, higher wages, social capital, decline in revenue, the existence or non-existence of local community facilities such as roads, streets, electricity, sewage and water facilities? The minister's statement does not reflect any consideration in this regard. Has the effect of the government's fumble bumble fiscal policy been taken into account? No, Mr. Speaker, it has not.

Labour Conditions
These items I have enumerated represent basic causes for the existence of the many depressed areas. In his statement the minister is proposing to disregard all of the factors. He says in effect: let us come up with a formula that will sound nice and read well in the newspapers and hope it will be acceptable to the country before it finds out that we have hoodwinked it, and before it finds out that we do not have much concern for the difficulties which exist.
The economic decay that has existed in some communities as a result of chronic unemployment will certainly not lead to the attraction of industry to those communities regardless of the double depreciation of which the minister speaks. This is a malignant social sickness that exists in some areas of chronic unemployment resulting from the factors I have mentioned. Some industries will not locate in areas regardless of the chronic unemployment and regardless of the incentive of a depreciation nature put forward on behalf of the government. Industry will always look for a community or area in the light of existing facilities such as transportation, communication, closeness to markets and natural resources, living and social conditions, roads, bridges, electricity, sewerage systems and the like. Those are the factors which influence the location of industry rather than this double-talk about double depreciation. The double depreciation will have much less ininfluence on the location of industry than will the existence of the facilities I have outlined.
This announcement is a great disappointment which has been foisted upon parliament and the people of Canada. Apart from the fact that his department is obviously unable to cope with the economic situation, and apart from the fact that it may help in some small way, this stingy policy of the Minister of Finance is a great disappointment. Double depreciation on a set formula varying only as between 75 per cent and 50 per cent in regard to the over-10,000 population areas and under-10,000 population areas is based on the assumption that every depressed area in Canada is equal in so far as concerns the conditions resulting in chronic depression, but this is not a fair approach. It is true that these areas are equal in so far as the depression is concerned, but it is not true that they are equal in so far as the cause of the depression are concerned except for the fact that the people in the areas are living under a Conservative government.

Surely there exist somewhere in a government agency or in the Department of Labour itself, individuals who are capable of dealing with this question. We must have an assessment of the causes of unemployment which lead to the chronic depressed areas. We need an assessment and investigation of the causes for these areas becoming chronic depressed areas. We must find an answer based on the elements of the unemployment, not an answer directed to creating incentive. The second suggestion I would make, and we have been advocating this for many years, is the creation of a national development council with money and authority at its disposal which could base its actions upon the results of inquiries, which are necessary in order to improve the situation.

the motion before us cannot deal with remedies for unemployment. This is obviously so, because the plan announced yesterday does not deal with remedies either. I agree wholeheartedly with that suggestion.
Inasmuch as I am prevented from going into the positive field because of the objection of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who obviously does not wish positive suggestions to be made because they are embarrassing to a government that has none of its own, I will deal very briefly with the criteria themselves.
I mentioned that the reason they are restrictive is that they assume that in all cases the reasons are the same. They take the months of the year in which there is likely to be the lowest level of unemployment. They take a sufficient period of time so that the bad years under the Tories, when we had high unemployment in the summer, will be counterbalanced by the years preceding them when there was less unemployment in the summer
If you are going to use a statistical system,
I suggest this should happen. Perhaps I could make reference to the announcement of the minister yesterday. He said that the second requirement, in so far as areas over 10,000 are concerned, is that industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-60. I say that condition should be eliminated. I say that because it is one of those conditions which will very seldom be met, if there is any truth in the remarks made previously by the minister that employment has been increasing. I say this condition should be eliminated and should not be part of the statistical requirement.
In so far as areas of less than 10,000 are concerned, I do not know what the difference is between these two references, but one refers to the fact that industrial employment conditions must have generally deteriorated over the years. I do not know whether that means over the eight years mentioned, over the years to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred, or to what years it does refer. But in any event this should not be part of the statistical requirement. It is restrictive and will prevent many areas from participating.
In so far as the 75 per cent and 50 per cent are concerned, this government would be much closer to dealing with the problem and would be much more able to gloat about what it does if it were to take a straight percentage figure of the total labour force in the area as compared, perhaps, with the national figure. The government should take a total figure of, say, 4 per cent or 5 per cent as a yearly figure and then deal with it on

that basis, rather than, as I said earlier, practically repealing the plan before it even comes into effect.

speechtext:
Coming as I do from the constituency of Bow River, I am interested in this motion because of a particular situation which exists in that area. May I say, first of all, that I am well aware of the terms and conditions of the present debate. I know this is a motion which, in effect, criticizes the conditions set out by the Minister of Labour on November 2 last with regard to the application of double depreciation allowances to certain localities. I can speak with some feeling on this subject because I come from an area where there has been unemployment in the coal mines for between ten and 15 years. I am referring to the Drumheller area.
These coal miners are engaged in mining what is known as soft domestic coal and because of competition from natural gas and petroleum fuels they have been thrown out of work and kept out of work for a number of years. So it is not my intention, as far as that situation is concerned, to blame anyone for what has occurred. Surely, what all of us should be asking is this: what can we do to help in a situation of this kind? Let us make no mistake about it. The situation as far as unemployment is concerned existed when this government took office; and I am sure as I stand in my place today that the workers of this country whether they live in western Canada or in the rest of Canada have confidence in the Minister of Labour and in this government.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Call an election and let us find out.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
We have heard that cry about calling an election before. The opposition asked us to call an election in 1958 and

Labour Conditions
the C.C.F. almost got wiped out. It is only by the grace of God that a few of them are left.
Returning to the terms of the motion, I think this would be a good time to review exactly what the Minister of Labour said in reference to the criteria which have to be established in connection with this double depreciation allowance. He said this as reported in Hansard on page 2569:
Hon. members will recall that one objective of this program is to assist new industries in areas where there has been a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years.
That is the first point I wish to make. There has been substantial unemployment over the years in the area of Drumheller where the coal miners have been mining soft domestic fuel. The Minister of Labour has come to grips with the situation and set criteria defining those areas to which we intend that industry should be attracted. No one is going to say in this house today that there are no areas in which serious unemployment exists. There was serious unemployment in 1955 and in 1957 and there is serious unemployment in 1961. There is, too, serious unemployment in the United States, as the hon. member for Essex East mentioned last night when we were discussing this subject.
The areas affected are broken down into two categories: areas with a labour force of 10,000 and over, and areas with a labour force of less than 10,000. In the minister's statement we find the following:
In those areas where the labour force is 10,000 and over the criteria are, first, the area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category for 75 per cent or more of the summer months from May to October, 1953-60.
That is the first criterion applying to the first group. Here is the second one:
Second, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-60.
Those are the criteria in the first category set out by the minister on March 2. Let us take the second category, that of areas with a labour force of less than 10,000. In the first place, these must have been classified by the Department of Labour as in a surplus labour market category for 50 per cent or more of the 48 summer months May to October, 195360. In the second place, industrial employment conditions must have generally deteriorated over the years.
Last, but not least, applications may be made by the municipal authorities. That is the part of the statement with which I want to deal for a few minutes. If we set out in law those areas to which this formula should apply, it would be too rigid and there would be no flexibility. That is the very thing about

which some of my hon. friends in the corner spoke with respect to another matter. They thought it was not flexible enough.
If you attempt to set out in law specific, designated areas there is no question but that it would be highly improbable that you could designate all the areas without missing one or two or more and would make bad exceptions. That is the point.
Under the present proposals the question will be handled in a democratic way with the initiative and suggestions flowing from the municipal level to the federal level. After all, in the democratic system it is important that all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, co-operate for the common good. Who knows local conditions better than do those at the municipal level? The municipalities can and may make application on the basis of their knowledge of the local conditions.
Let us take the municipality of Drumheller as an example. They have already written me as their member expressing the hope that the application will be placed with the appropriate officials as soon as possible so they can comply with the stated criteria. That, to me, seems to be a point that argues strongly in favour of the criteria as set out by the Minister of Labour. If the measure is approved by parliament it will make a significant contribution in attracting industry to depressed centres and in creating additional employment opportunities.
There is, however, a second point which I feel is very important. The introduction of this measure illustrates that the government demonstrates its belief in the freedom of enterprise. The government believes in the ability of free enterprise to solve the problems of unemployment. It has demonstrated this belief by giving an advantage to industry. Through the advantage of double depreciation industry can enlarge and expand their capital. Industry will be attracted to various areas and that in itself will create employment in those areas that need it. I do not think we should lose sight of those two facts to which I have referred.
The subject which is being debated this afternoon is one which was dealt with last night by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and if it is in order to talk about it at all, it is surely in order for me to comment on what the hon. gentleman said. In so doing, in all likelihood I will be dealing with the subject he touched upon.
The hon. member's criticism of this measure was that the criteria do not go far enough. The hon. gentleman suggested that we should have followed the course followed by President Kennedy in designating specific areas

as depressed areas. I remind hon. gentlemen of the Liberal party of the fact that there will be greater flexibility as a result of the manner in which the Minister of Labour has handled this matter. The criteria introduced by the minister will make the formula flexible and workable.
I observed that the hon. member for Essex East pounded his desk when I made mention of the course followed by President Kennedy. I suppose that the hon. gentleman likes the victory of President Kennedy. We all like to see people successful in politics and particularly we Conservatives because we were successful in 1957 and again in 1958. Just as President Kennedy was successful in the recent United States election so our national leader was successful in 1957 and 1958.
Of course, it is an old trick of the Liberals to applaud success. They were happy to climb on the coat tails of Roosevelt so they could get back in power in 1935. Of course, this is not a new trick and the reason why hon. gentlemen opposite refer in terms of praise to the proposal of President Kennedy is that my hon. friends have nothing new to offer. With respect to the unemployment problem my hon. friends have nothing to offer at all.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; when you hear me out, you will see I am in order. What I am saying is that my hon. friends in the Liberal party have no alternative to the criteria suggested by the Minister of Labour and therefore they naturally want to climb on the coat tails of president Kennedy in the hope that in the future they may become victorious in an election in Canada and form the government. My hon. friends are not interested in solving the unemployment problem or in suggesting constructive proposals or altenatives.
Are my hon. friends absolutely and flatly opposed to the criteria suggested by the Minister of Labour? Do they say this formula will not solve the problems in those areas where there is serious unemployment?

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I heard the comment of the hon. member for Essex East and it is important because as I understood the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon, he did not criticize the purport of this measure but said we were wrong in the fact that we did not designate certain areas. The hon. gentleman did not really find fault
Labour conditions
with the criteria but said that we should have designated areas and not placed the onus on the municipalities.
My answer to that occupation-and I will repeat it-is that we believe that the local levels of government are important in democracy. For the federal government to designate areas would be imposing dictatorship from the top level down to the bottom level. Suggestions should come from the bottom to the top and so we have in this proposal a true example of democracy in operation in this country.
I now return to my argument. It seems to me the crux of the situation is that the hon. gentlemen opposite do not argue that the criteria are inadequate but that they protest the way in which the proposal is going to be administered. Let us examine how it will be administered.
In my opening remarks I said that I felt the workers in this country have confidence in the Minister of Labour. I believe the minister, as he has in the past, will prove his ability to administer this proposal accurately and justly. After all, in dealing with a scheme of this nature and magnitude, we have to have expert administrators to administer the laws and that is why the formula should be flexible. If the depressed areas were categorically set out in law the formula would not be as flexible as it otherwise would be; in that way bad exceptions and bad examples would creep in and problems would be created.
Let me return to my own area of Drum-heller about which I spoke earlier. The municipality can make an application. If the application of that area is approved, industry will be attracted to that centre and the coal miners who have been out of work over the years can find employment in another industry and live with their families in dignity.
I should like to cite this as an example. When I went to that area in 1955-1956 I saw large numbers of houses of the miners boarded up and the mines closed down. There was and is a surplus labour pool in that area. That surplus labour pool is looking for new industries in that area. It is for that reason that I rose this afternoon to speak in support of this remedy for unemployment and in support of the criteria that have been set out by the Minister of Labour. The result of the passage of this measure will closely affect the people I represent in the community of Drumheller and those in Canmore, Alberta.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in the debate on this subject, but that was before the announcement was made by the

minister to deal with areas which he has the new industries which we have attracted styled as areas of surplus manpower. How- employ only five or six people. Weekly and ever, I am required to rise to protest the monthly the figures mount. The government definition of the criteria which have been listens not to the cries from this and similar
placed before us as anything which is indicative of an acceptance by the government of its responsibility in answer to those in need in various communities in Canada.
On a previous occasion I have styled as a depressed area the riding which I have the honour to represent. This has met with incredulity on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and with indifference on the part of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr).
We have before us not a formula to assist depressed areas but, at the very best, a formula to assist in disaster areas. If any area can qualify under the criteria presented to this house yesterday, it must be an area so badly hit already that this crumb which the government offers can in no way assist in its economic recovery.
There are many areas such as those I represent, and particularly the two larger areas of Fort Erie and Niagara Falls. They are, or were, largely industrial. One of their industries, of course, is the tourist industry which is most important in the summer months. Were my area in a position to qualify under the government's criteria, the fact that we have an influx of tourist dollars coming into the country in the summertime for a period of two or three months every year removes them from what the government will now be describing as an area of surplus manpower.
Nevertheless, over the past three or four years the number of unemployed has continued to rise. I refer to the chronically unemployed. The Minister of Labour visited my riding as recently as October of last year. I have already placed on Hansard the minister's remarks at that time and the fact that he said he intended to do something for the people in that area. Apparently the sort of thing which he intends to do in this riding and indeed in that represented by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) is, at times of election, to throw in one contract but otherwise disregard the people of the area.
I would suggest that this government has indicated no way of assisting particular areas such as mine where a certain industry is in serious trouble. In my riding the silver industry, the workers on the railroads and in the aircraft industry in particular are suffering and increasingly so. It is true that we have attracted some industries, are still attracting them. However, we have plants which have been employing as many as 2,500 people and which are now down to 250 employees; and

areas. I think this is another indication that this government and in particular the Minister of Labour have neglected and forgotten that which they are so proud of, namely their humble origin. Perhaps nothing in the world has been seen to equal the arrogance of this government and its indifference to the people since Marie Antoinette said, "Let them eat cake".
I suggest to the government that if, as was indicated in the speech that was made on December 20 last, this government has a real interest in the people and in assisting particularly areas which have been affected by a number of economic factors, what is now offered is just not enough. In fact, I would suggest to the government that there is not one area in Canada which can qualify under this criterion. I would further suggest that it is interesting to know that the government has taken the period from the year 1953. If the government v/ill amend its criterion in order to take it back only to the summer of 1957, it will be in a better position to tell how many depressed areas there are in this country under this administration.
I have little to say, Mr. Speaker, nor can I expect any consideration for the people I represent or indeed the people of Canada. However, I would entreat the Minister of Labour to rise in his place and give us his views rather than to leave it to the fringe area of his party to speak on this most important issue. I would ask the Minister of Labour to detail to us the areas in Ontario and in each of the provinces his experts in the Department of Labour have told him this formula will apply to, if any. I challenge the government to indicate that there is any area which will qualify under this criterion. I ask the government to consider the fact that the municipality-for it is the municipality which must apply-must call itself a depressed area. I ask the minister also to consider that when it calls itself a depressed area it is likely to drive away prospective new business, new industries and new residents. It is likely to frighten away any sort of industry. When that area feels that it needs special assistance it throws itself upon the government and says, "We are depressed; assist us", and then finds that it is not only necessary to be depressed but to be destroyed in order for the regulations to take effect.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that in this particular parliament there is a coherent attempt, which I think is praiseworthy, on the part of the

government to give to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and his department a larger role in the economy. I have been complimentary before, and I may still be complimentary to the minister for making positive public statements in the past that this government accepted the responsibility for unemployment in this country and was prepared to face that responsibility. But this acceptance of responsibility, it seems to me, indicates a need to have some procedure by which the problem can be met.
It seems to me that the two main sources of power and influence in our economic pattern in this country in the federal government have been in the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance. Therefore I, like I am sure a number of other hon. members, have been waiting to see a shift to the Department of Labour that will enable it to give the leadership in facing the unemployment problem that the Minister of Labour has conceded. All I can say about these regulations, following the statement of the Minister of Finance, is that it is very apparent that the shift of power to the Department of Labour is not taking place in any effective way. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) or the Department of Finance is still holding the course.
My first point about these regulations is that they are a very minor concession. This has already been underlined by the Leader of the Opposition, but what kind of concession is it to give double depreciation for one year out of any three years? In essence, it is a pittance when compared with the concession that the mining companies have in Canada. I think it does work as an incentive to give the concession and to have no income tax or corporation tax on the first three years of operation. It seems to me that kind of incentive, because it is both general and generous, has had some real effect as compared with this very narrow concession.
One of the other factors about this concession, it seems to me, is that it ignores the places in Canada where capital accumulates and from which it is controlled. If the area of Sydney qualifies for this assistance-and according to the statistics I have been able to find, it might qualify; it is right on the boundary line-where is the corporate structure in Canada that has the capital that is going to take advantage of the situation in Sydney to get the double depreciation? I insist that that capital is in the main controlled in and the exploitation takes place from the large metropolitan centres such as Montreal and Toronto.
If one takes a map something like the one I hold in my hand, which sets out the labour surplus problem and clearly marks the labour
Labour Conditions
areas, 1953 to 1959, one has to speculate on large organizations such as Abitibi or Mc-Intyre-Porcupine, looking at this map and saying, "Oh, there is a dark area; surely the one marked is the one where we can get double depreciation; that is where we will go and set up a plant". I think this is incredibly naive when I think of my own area and all of the persistent attempts that have been made by the northwestern Ontario development association, the integrated chambers of commerce, both of Port Arthur and Fort William, and of northwestern Ontario to get industries to come in. These people have made movies and shown them all over Europe and the United States. They have sent off representatives at their own expense, paid for with money that they raised themselves. They have sent them all over the United States and Europe in order to make contacts and to get industry to come into their area; yet in the main, as far as I can discover, despite all this tremendous effort, in the last five years, we have had almost no new industries. I know that in 1960 we obtained at the head of the lakes one new industry, a concrete culvert plant that employs four people. My point in this is that we have had a region that is marked off roughly by the Department of Labour as a certain area, Port Arthur and Fort William, that has had a tremendous need for initiative and drive. I am not a man to suggest-

It will be the corporation that will take advantage of it. I have tried to explain that our region has gone out after industry and has not been able to get it to come in. I am suggesting that the corporate structure of our country is such, with power concentrated in certain places and in certain organizations, that you have to offer something much more attractive than this provision in order to get corporations to move into these areas.

I have gone through the statistics in connection with labour and the information which has been filed before the Senate committee, and I find that my particular region will not qualify under these particular criteria. My point is, Mr. Speaker, that here is an area that knows it is in deep trouble. It has tried to do something on its own initiative. It has requested incentives but the criteria that have been introduced by the Minister of Labour really do not mean very much to this area.
Aside from the fact that the incentive itself is insufficient, one must consider that we are dealing with percentages that vary up and down and that they must be related to the past. It seems to me that you have to have a most marked trend, an almost completely hopeless situation, before you can hope to get any advantage from the criteria that have been established in this provision. I insist that we have in Canada today a number of regions that are right on the edge of this test, and ours is one that could not qualify under this 1953-1960 standard. We have an annual average of 10 per cent of the registrants for employment who are unemployed; that is the average. The percentage over this particular period is not quite high enough to qualify us as a surplus labour area. The reason this area cannot qualify during the summer months is the change that has taken place in the woods industry. In former years employment in the woods was concentrated

in the wintertime, but within the last few years that period has changed to the summertime.
The other thing about these criteria, Mr. Speaker, is that they make no allowance for what are universally acknowledged to be the new reasons that we are having labour surplus areas. This is what is known as structural unemployment, and it comes upon a region fairly quickly. The power saw, in effect, has been the greatest revolutionizer in our industry, but in 1953 the power saw was not an important factor. However, since 1956 and 1957 it has changed the whole bush employment picture in our area. There have been other developments such as the carry-lift loader, drop loaders and what we call slashmobiles which have been introduced within the last few years and have cut the need for workers. However, the effects of these developments will not be reflected in the criteria we have here.
I was talking the other day to the head of one of our iarge labour unions, the northwestern Ontario lumber and sawmill workers union. He was saying that a few years ago they had 17,000 members. This is a tough mill and trade union which is feared, respected and hated in various sections of our part of the country. It is not a trade union that allows the membership to get away very easily. No one has come in and taken away any of the members; there have been no raids or jurisdictional squabbles. However, during the last four years the membership has dropped from 17,000 to about 11,000 today. I am not saying that they are protesting the changes that have taken place in the woods industry in our area, but their membership is going to go even lower. They are not squawking about this particular situation. What happens to the men who are uprooted and put in a difficult position? As a result of this our whole economy in northwestern Ontario has been affected by these changes in the woods operations in the last few years as well as the dieselization that has taken place on the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific.
The Minister of Labour knows very well that dieselization has only become a crippling factor in employment terms within the last two or three years. In my constituency there are eight different railway divisional points, so the magnitude of the effect of dieselization upon employment is very apparent there. However, this factor, again, will not be reflected in the period 1953-1960 with any great effectiveness. This particular region is considered to be, then, from what I can

gather, a normal labour market area. However, we know that it is not. This is the difficulty when you set up criteria that go away back into the past.
I recall how critical I felt when listening to some of the farmers who were criticizing the agricultural prices stabilization board setup and the fact that prices were going to be set on the basis of a 10-year period. Some hon. members were pointing out the inequity of this, but that provision related to inanimate objects, farm products. The problem with which we are faced here relates to human beings. You have to deal with it with much more compassion than you do with such things as butter and eggs. I suggest that the measure is just not good enough; but if that is out of order, I suggest the criteria are much too severe to be useful to us. I know, Mr. Speaker, that much feeling will be aroused over this in our part of the country.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the fact that Cornwall qualifies under these criteria. I hope this does Cornwall some good. But what about all the other places in Canada that are going to be just below Cornwall and will not qualify? The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) was talking about flexibility and how much flexibility we have here. All I can say about the marvelous criteria is that they delimit the provision and make it so narrow that an area has to be in an almost helpless position before it can receive any assistance from the proposal of the Minister of Labour.
There is one last point I want to touch on, Mr. Chairman, and that is the point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). He has mentioned the fact that he has received no response from members of this party in relation to the specific unemployment problem that exists in Cape Breton. 1 might say to the member that I have received his correspondence but have not as yet answered because-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. I do not think that subject is a proper one to discuss on the motion that is before the house.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I just mention this because the hon. member brought the subject to my attention this afternoon. 1 had no intention of interrupting the hon. member at the time but wanted to mention why I had not written to him. I took the matter into consideration, discussed it with the manager of a local thermal plant and was informed by the manager that the suggestion of importing coal from Cape Breton to Port Arthur was a fantastic one in view of the fact that the source of United States coal is much closer. I have no influence with the Hon.
Labour Conditions
Leopold Macauley or Premier Frost and would assume, party ties being what they are, that the hon. member for Cape Breton South would be much more able to accomplish something in this regard through his own party structure than through me.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not at all surprised to find that the opposition posed today and presented a motion to the effect that the criteria set up for double depreciation in certain areas in this country are inadequate and of a restrictive character. This is something that we as a government expected. We have been endeavouring to do everything possible to put forward measures and legislation in this house since November 17, 1959, to help alleviate the situation. We find every time that members of the opposition rise as one with the cry that this is not enough and is restrictive. They have done this on some twenty five occasions since November 17th. When there is an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, for the opposition to approve or disapprove they rise as one and say, yes, it is a good measure but it is not enough. I am not surprised of course in this regard; that is the job of the opposition. It does not matter what the government brings forward, the cry is always the same: it is not enough, it does not go far enough, it does not include enough area, even though we must bring in measure after measure to deal with the situation.
The measure that was announced yesterday is designed to help certain areas in this country. The criteria may be criticized. There could be 1,001 different criteria. This is not criticism in regard to the criteria put forward by the government alone; this criticism will be put forward in any case. We are criticized in regard to this criteria being wrong. It is suggested that we should use some other criteria instead. This is the type of criticism we have heard today. I gave three examples of localities in Canada which I said-stressing very emphatically-that they might qualify under this criteria. Today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) says that already he has received communications from right across this country to the effect that the writers do not understand these criteria. Mr. Speaker, I have not received any communication from any area or municipality to that effect at all. I believe that this statement in regard to the receipt of letters is made in order that something critical of this measure is brought forward.
I feel that the Leader of the Opposition is doing an injustice to Elliot Lake in saying that in his opinion Elliot Lake cannot qualify under these criteria. Surely, the Leader of the Opposition should not undermine the thinking

Labour Conditions
of the municipal authorities by saying they cannot qualify under these criteria. I think this is an injustice. Certainly the municipality of Elliot Lake has every right, as any other municipal area in this country has, to make an application to the Department of Labour which will investigate, along with the officials of the national employment service very rapidly, the situation in order to ascertain whether the applicant area qualifies for double depreciation, as set forth, for industries which locate in the area.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) has also stated that she does not feel that Niagara Falls would qualify. I would suggest that if it does not qualify, that is all to the good. Why should an area such as Niagara Falls qualify when it has experienced the expansion of industry that many other municipalities have not experienced for some years? Just a few moments ago we had figures produced in regard to the industrial development in that area. We heard about the encouragements put forward in an attempt to attract new industry, with a fair amount of success. We are very happy that Niagara Falls is an area that is progressing, and that industry feels it can locate in the area.
We have heard criticism in regard to the summer months limitation. The reason for this requirement, Mr. Speaker, is obvious. The seasonal unemployment in winter months would have a great effect on the situation. If we intend to get a true picture in regard to unemployment declining generally we must consider the employment situation during months when the seasonal aspect is not evident.
Before I go on I might say a few words in regard to the statement respecting the measures announced by President Kennedy in the United States. All the credit in the world should be given to him for implementing the proposals he has made. I am sure I would be out of order, Mr. Speaker, if I dwelt and enlarged upon a comparison of the measures taken by the two countries; but if I were to make such a comparison it would be interesting to note that of the 12 immediate measures proposed by the President of the United States we would find, Mr. Speaker, that here in Canada 11 have already been put forward. As I say, I will not go further with that comparison because I feel I certainly would be out of order. However, I would certainly enjoy the opportunity at this time of making a comparison of each and every one of those measures.
The motion before us today is a peculiar one. The opposition has moved the adjournment of the house because of the exception they have taken, Mr. Speaker, to certain criteria set up by the government in its

announcement of the policy for permitting double depreciation in certain areas that request it. What lies behind this motion, Mr. Speaker, is the opposition's desire and determination that the government shall in this Canada of ours set up certain areas as depressed or distressed areas; and from their point of view, the more depressed and distressed they are, the better.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The minister has just said that it is our view and position that the more depressed and distressed an area is, the better. These words are entirely false and I ask the minister to withdraw them.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Leader of the Opposition assures me that that is not their intention, and that is not what is behind this motion, then I certainly do withdraw those remarks. Certainly that was the inference I drew from what was said yesterday, which was out of order, and again today. It certainly gave me that impression.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: A false impression.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
However, if the Leader of the Opposition says that is not true, then of course I withdraw that charge. But the opposition seems to be determined to take this undemocratic approach to the problem. It is certainly not the approach that has been prevalent in this country, whereby there is a certain amount of respect for those governments which are not at the high level of the federal government. The opposition says that we, as the federal government, should tell municipalities and areas, "Here you are. We put a stigma upon you, whether you want it or not, and designate you as a depressed area". That word was used by the opposition.
I have been connected with municipal affairs for nine years, and I know that other hon. members presently in this house have been connected with that level of government. I know they will agree with me that this is a matter for consideration by the municipal authorities. It is a matter for the municipal authorities and the elected members of those municipalities to determine. When they have determined that in their opinion they qualify to have industry brought into their areas, then the way is open to them to apply to the Department of Labour. At that time representatives from the Department of Labour and the national employment service will make a thorough examination. If they qualify, they will be so designated by order in council, and only then. I think that is a fair approach to this problem.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
minister a question. He has mentioned one

point which I raised. Is the minister now saying that there will be a separate order in council for each municipality designated as an area of surplus labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the area or locality will be designated by order in council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Each one?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Whether it will be a separate order in council or whether two or three areas might be included in one order in council is a matter that will depend on the circumstances. If we receive a report simultaneously from two or three areas that qualify, then I think we could cut down on our orders in council by designating them in one order in council.
There must be a basis upon which to set criteria. How were these criteria arrived at? Since January, 1953, every month the Department of Labour has classified labour market areas according to the degree of manpower utilization in various areas across this country. Because the labour market classifications of the Department of Labour have been published since 1953, it was felt they would be more acceptable than any other approach which might be devised for this purpose.
Since 1953 labour market areas have been classified into four groups: substantial surplus, moderate surplus, balance, and labour shortage. In the criteria used for classifying surplus manpower areas, the term "surplus labour market" refers to both the substantial surplus and the moderate surplus classifications.
I submit that this motion has been brought about in order to say once again that the measure is no good. That has been the case with other measures that this government has brought forward, as it has promised to do, and it will continue to bring forward measures to alleviate the situation. That is why the opposition says these are not the proper criteria. They say, "If we had been asked, we would have given your criteria". It does not matter whether we have 1,001 criteria; there will always be something wrong with them. This government is trying to deal with the situation for the good of this country and for the good of the working man and woman of this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) began his remarks by stating that he was not surprised at the criticism levelled at the government for the policy which he announced yesterday. I must say to him now that I am extremely surprised at the reply he has made to the questions, suggestions and criticisms concerning that policy.
Labour Conditions

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member used the word "suggestions". I have yet to hear any suggestions as to the type of criteria that should have been adopted.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour could not have been listening, because the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) put on record a suggestion in connection with this matter. If the minister had been listening he would not have interrupted me a moment ago.
Coming back to this statement made by the Minister of Labour, I am indeed surprised that the minister did not take the opportunity to explain in greater detail and at greater length the so-called criteria to which he referred yesterday.
A number of members on the government side of the house have risen in support of this resolution, but has any member of the house, including the Minister of Labour, told us this afternoon what these criteria mean? The Minister of Labour had an opportunity to deal with this matter in the few minutes at his disposal. He could have taken the requisite time to tell us the meaning of this order in council, and he spoke for barely 12 minutes. Why did he not, as the minister responsible for this policy, explain in detail to the House of Commons what is meant by the criteria and by the division of the two categories?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If I had done so, would that have satisfied you?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is your job.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
We would at least have known what is in the mind of the government. As it is now, we certainly do not know what is in the mind of the government, because it is as clear as mud.
In the discussion of this motion of the Leader of the Opposition to adjourn the house reference was made to a statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) during the course of his supplementary budget speech on December 20, 1960. As found at page 1,007 of Hansard the Minister of Finance said at that time:
As a powerful incentive to these ends I am pleased to announce measures to fulfil three major purposes.
The Leader of the Opposition has put this on the record and I shall not repeat it. That was a positive statement by the Minister of Finance that powerful measures would be announced, and we had every right to believe that those powerful measures would soon be introduced in the House of Commons. But it took over two months for that to be done; and then it was done by this puny little measure,

Labour Conditions
this timid measure announced yesterday by the Minister of Labour. Not only were there very substantial and serious delays, but there was confusion because it was impossible for a long time to know which of three departments would be concerned with this matter.
That is why the Minister of Labour is so timid about the whole thing. The reason is quite clear. When this announcement was made on December 20 the government had not determined its policy. It was only later, I suggest, perhaps a day or two ago, that it was decided to follow this method which was announced in the house. That is why the matter has been thrown into the hands of the Minister of Labour, who should have been able to rise in his place this afternoon and explain to the people of Canada what is meant by these criteria. I say to the Minister of Labour that these criteria are unsatisfactory and that he should have explained to the house what was meant by them.
Who is going to designate the areas? The Minister of Labour in reply to criticism which was directed at him, when he stated that we had an undemocratic approach to the problem, asked: why should the municipalities not have the responsibility of making application? During the budget speech and during the course of debate on a number of occasions we had clear-cut statements by representatives of the government that they intended to assist those who were suffering from unemployment and that they were ready, also, to assist the depressed areas or areas of so-called chronic underunemployment. Why were not those undertakings carried out? Why was the stand taken in the budget speech and by other ministers in the course of debate not carried out save and except in the words of the Minister of Labour who so mildly attempted to reply to some of the criticisms which were made?
I believe the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) was quite right when she referred to a statement made by a former queen of France, "Let them have cake". I add to that a statement made by one of the ministers of the government, "Let them have bread or games, bread or circuses". That statement was made on more than one occasion and that is exactly what is happening in this situation. It seems to me that it is up to the Minister of Labour to take the initiative in designating areas which are entitled to these double depreciation allowances.
It has been said here that in order to assist industry to locate in a community certain advantages must be offered; and one of the advantages which the government proposes is a double depreciation allowance for a period of one year extending over a period of three years. How can an industry 
establish itself in a community when it does not know whether it will be entitled to the double depreciation allowance and cannot know until a decision has been confirmed by order in council? How long is it going to take before this information is available? How long will it take the municipalities to convince the Department of Labour or the governor in council that they qualify under these criteria? Moreover, the criteria are such that it is almost impossible for them to know what the position is.
The minister made great play about the fact that he had not stated that Elliot Lake and Springhill could qualify but had said they might qualify. Why should the minister not tell us whether they do qualify or not? If he or the officials of his department do not know, then how in the world can the municipalities of Elliot Lake, Springhill or Cornwall for that matter, which is in a difficult situation as the minister is aware, be expected to know?
The government and the Department of Labour have had three months in which to find out what the circumstances should be in the application of this formula, yet it is only yesterday that we had the announcement concerning it. I say to the minister that this formula is so restrictive that it leaves many communities in the lurch and outside the benefits, if there are any, which flow from the terms of this policy.
I think the Minister of Labour cannot avoid telling the house either now or at a later date what these areas are in order to avoid the delays which must otherwise attend the application of this policy. Where are these areas of chronic unemployment? Certainly the Minister of Finance during the course of his speech on the budget, in the course of answers to questions we asked in the house and in the course of other debates led us to believe that we should be given this information. There was no one on this side of the house who for a moment did not believe that this information would be forthcoming in clear and definite terms. As it is now, I challenge the minister to tell us what this thing means. Although, as I said earlier, two members who support the government have risen to tell us something about this proposal, to tell us they are in favour of it, no one, including the Minister of Labour himself, has told us in clear and definite language what these criteria mean and how they can be applied.
There is another matter about which I think the house should be informed and it concerns the manner in which this proposal is going to operate. I urge the minister and the government to change and improve these criteria which are faulty. We believe that

the figures of total population instead of paid workers should be used to calculate the percentage of unemployment, because our population statistics on a regional basis are much better than the figures on the paid workers basis. Moreover, the period selected is certainly unsatisfactory because it includes four summers of prosperity and four summers of recession. The period to be used should be the last three years because chronic unemployment really started at the end of 1957.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It certainly did. Look at the figures.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
During this debate the question has been asked: what can we do to solve this problem? We are all in support of what measures may be taken to solve this problem but I tell the government and its supporters that they will not solve it by this puny method. They will not solve anything by refusing to define what is meant by an area of chronic unemployment.
Another statement which has been made in the course of the debate is that the former administration is responsible for the present unemployment situation. Let me tell the house that the present government has now been in office for almost four years; and if the situation has reached the point which it has reached today, they and they alone are responsible for the conditions. They should be able to stand on their own feet and cease blaming an administration which has been out of office since 1957. But no; they are not prepared to do so. I notice that the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) who does not say very much in this house was down in the province of Quebec the other day saying that the high degree of unemployment in this country was the responsibility of the former government. I am telling members opposite that they will not solve the problem of unemployment by statements like this. They must do it by policies. They must do it by bringing in measures which they themselves said they were going to bring in. We waited for nearly three months for a definition of these areas and we had it only yesterday.
I was saying that the period to be used should be the last three years, because chronic unemployment actually started at the end of 1957. If you look at the figures, Mr. Speaker, you will see that unemployment in this country then was very little over 3 per cent. Areas may have enjoyed prosperity and boom conditions between 1953 and 1957 but after 1957 they may have experienced heavy unemployment. In that case they would not qualify under the government's program. That
Labour Conditions
is another fault which we on this side have to find with the summer months definition. It is well known to every member in this house that during the period 1953-56 if not, 195357, there were boom conditions in certain areas of this country. That certainly was the case, in large part, in the city of Cornwall because of the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, but after that because of the closing down of several cotton industries no less than 2,000 people were put out of work. Reading this definition as carefully as I can I am still unable to say whether or not that community will be able to qualify. I am also sure the minister is unable to say and certainly he has thrown no light on it today.
I submit that the definition of the two categories, the one having to do with an area with a labour force of 10,000 and over, and the other having to do with one with a labour force of 10,000 and under, should be more clearly set out by the government. On the basis of the statement put on the record by the Leader of the Opposition I think it is clear that it is going to be almost impossible to determine how a community with a labour force of under 10,000 will be able to apply. In the case of the category of a labour force of 10,000 and under the situation will be unworkable as was pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition and by others who have spoken.
In his remarks the Minister of Labour said that the government is bringing in measure after measure to deal with the unemployment situation. I am not free, any more than was the minister, to deal with those measures because of the restriction in the debate but I have yet to see brought in by the government since the session opened in 1960 a measure that will deal with the unemployment situation during the course of the present winter. Surely the present measure is not one which will be of much use during the course of the present winter season, because after an application is made time will be required to consider and study it and the industry in the community which will be waiting will want to be given some advance notice of whether or not it will be entitled to double depreciation.
I ask the Minister of Labour and hon. members of the government what industry is going to be tremendously enticed to come into a community if it will receive only one year of double depreciation during a period of three years, unless it is already there and wants to add to its facilities. That is what the Minister of Finance called a powerful incentive. If it is a powerful incentive, it was weakly and inadequately defended by the Minister of Labour.

Labour Conditions
I say to the minister that even now he should tell the house what the areas are; and unless and until the hon. gentleman does that I submit to him with deference that it will be practically impossible for those municipalities who want to make an application to know where they stand.
It seems to me it is the responsibility of the government in office to take action and instead of exercising that responsibility it has shifted it on the municipality. The government is saying in effect to each municipality: "You tell us whether or not you are a depressed area; we do not know. But having regard to the two criteria that were placed on Hansard you tell us whether or not you are a depressed area and, if you qualify under our criteria, then we will perhaps act under the circumstances."
In his statement yesterday, as reported at page 2569 of Hansard, the Minister of Labour stated the criteria as being these:
-first, the area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category for 75 per cent or more of the 48 summer months from May to October, 1953-1960. Second, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-1960.
Who is going to satisfy the government that industrial employment has declined if during four of the years there is a boom of employment, then suddenly it disappears and there are serious conditions which indicate a substantial deterioration in the community? Who is going to make that determination? Is the onus on the municipality? Must the municipality prove a prima facie case before it can be qualified under these criteria or are the officials of the Department of Labour to determine that matter?

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has just asked me a question. In reply let me say I think I set that out very clearly in my statement yesterday and again in my remarks this afternoon. I said that upon receipt of an application the officials of the Department of Labour and of the national employment service will go to that municipality, make assessments at first hand and ascertain very quickly whether the municipality qualifies under the criteria.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is satisfactory.

subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am being asked what I want and I will tell the minister. The minister has the figures right here in the Department of Labour. The minister need not tell me that he does not know what the position is

in every Canadian community as far as labour is concerned. If the minister does not know, he certainly should know. The hon. gentleman has those figures. Those figures are in the possession of the minister and he should be the one to take the responsibility instead of shifting on the municipality the onus of proving a prima facie case as to whether or not industry has deteriorated in that area. I certainly do not accept that explanation from the minister.
If the Minister of Labour does not have the figures he certainly can obtain some of them from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), some from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and still others from the Minister of Finance. The figures are all here in various departments of government.
If the government had wanted to do so it could, of its own volition have determined all these questions beforehand; but instead of doing that the government is going to waste a lot of time and has shifted the responsibility to the municipalities in asking them to tell the government whether or not they are depressed areas. That is why we repeat now what we have said so often: It is too little and too late. You have been talking now about all the great things you were going to do-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Address the Chair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSED AREAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
You were talking about them in the speech from the throne. Hon. members of the government during the course of various debates repeated ad nauseum what the government was going to do to meet the unemployment problem. This is another step in that program and from what has been said I presume it is the last step for the time being at least. All these items are supposed to assist in meeting the unemployment problem.
I repeat what I said a moment ago. Again I urge two things upon the minister. I urge that he clarify still further either by a statement in this house or outside what is meant by the criteria and that he take into consideration the other suggestions I made a moment ago.

This is only typical of what I would expect from some of those opposition members, some of those centralizers, who would impose on municipalities even without their consent the stigma of depressed areas. It is important that the municipalities themselves, which are in a position to know best their needs, have the onus to determine whether it is more to their benefit to have this double depreciation as an inducement to attract new industries or whether it may be counterbalanced by the adverse publicity attracted to the area. I have personal experience of this particular problem. Some weeks ago a Toronto paper published what I would say was a lengthy prejudicial article on my home town of Cornwall with the headline, "Cornwall, City of Idle Men". I must say that many people in my area took great and violent exception to this adverse and to some extent unwarranted publicity, although far be it from me to underestimate the degree of the consequent damage of unemployment either in my area or in others. However, I think that point must be clear.
This government is not going to impose any stigma on municipalities. They themselves must decide what is in their best interest and act accordingly. They are the ones who must initiate this aspect of the matter. If they decide that it is to their benefit to do so, I have no doubt that the Minister of Labour will give them every assistance in providing the necessary statistics to substantiate their case; but the onus must be where it should be, namely on those independent units of government, which are the root and base of the democratic organization of government.
Finally, if every community is going to be entitled to double depreciation, if every community has this additional inducement to attract industry, then those areas which require it most will not derive any special advantage. As I understand it, the chief reason for this legislation is that those whose need is greatest derive the maximum advantage; in other words, they derive some special advantage to attract industries into areas where they are most needed.
This whole process of decentralization of industry is long overdue and very necessary for the over-all health and balance of the national economy. There should be a large measure of decentralization, and this is one measure directed toward that end. I repeat, if every community is entitled to this special attraction, those who deserve it most will
Labour Conditions
not derive any special benefit from it and the whole purpose of the legislation will be defeated. Presumably, from the facetious criticism of this legislation, it would appear that this is what the opposition is demanding, either inadvertently or by design.
I repeat, those areas which need these special inducements most are the ones which should receive full benefit from them. Obviously, if everybody gets them there is no special advantage to any area. I insist that this government had this matter obviously very much at heart when it devised this criterion having to do with the special benefit of double depreciation. Also, the thing that this government would never adopt is a dictatorial centralizing policy of imposing, if you want to call it that, the stigma or designation of depressed area on any community without that community's consent, or without that community knowing and saying that it is in its best interests that such be done and initiating action for the government to follow.
