speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-14, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (application to civil service).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is getting to be a sort of perennial bill of mine. Its primary design has been explained in other years; it is to make the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act applicable to employees in the public service, with certain exceptions which I will enumerate in a moment.
The provisions of the act would apply to the employees in the public service in so far as certification of a bargaining agent is concerned. It would make applicable also the provisions relating to the negotiation of collective agreements, the conciliation procedures and the like except in so far as the operation of the conciliation board is concerned, and except in so far as strike action is concerned. I will explain all this in a moment.
The current procedure, which has been in existence for many years for that matter, is for the various organizations representing the employees in the public service to prepare demands, as it were, or requests, to the government in office for adjustments in their salary structure, hours of work, holidays and the like, and then to wait in attendance, with cap in hand, usually upon the minister of finance or the cabinet itself to make up his or its mind.
Last year we saw what I considered to be a most unfortunate system of establishing the salary structures of civil servants in that certain groups were selected for particular increases which were at variance with increases granted to other groups of employees, and in certain instances no adjustments whatever were made. This leads to a situation in which charges could be made of favouritism or of lack of knowledge on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) or somebody else in attempting to bring the various salary structures of the various groups and types of employees in the public service into equity. In my opinion, it is the fundamental right of employees of any employer in this nation to be able to form into a union or an association, whatever they might call it, and to find through that union or association a means of solving the problems that arise as a result of their working conditions.
I do not believe we should draw too much distinction, although apparently in some instances it is desirous or necessary to do so,

between employees who work in the public service of Canada, or what is classified as the civil service, and employees who work in industry or for crown corporations. However, a distinction is made. The employees of crown corporations and of private industry are able to band together and form a collective unit, apply for certification and sit down with their employers to negotiate collectively the terms of an agreement or contract covering their wages, hours, working conditions and the like. Employees in the public service do not have this right.
The employees in the public service are and have been considered by the government as being in a sort of second class position. They do not have the rights, privileges and responsibilities of other employees in society, namely those working in private industry or those working for crown corporations. This situation does not apply to wages alone, although I suppose in a material society this would be the first consideration of employees. There are other matters to be considered such as grievances, conditions of employment, hours of work, holidays, vacations with pay, sick leave, seniority rights and so on. All of these things form part of an employee's working conditions.
Apart from the fact this is a contradiction of our concept of that phrase made famous by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), "human rights and fundamental freedoms". I think it is bad psychology for a group of employees to have no outlet for their feelings in so far as management is concerned, nc method of redress for their grievances, nc manner of attaining what they consider tc be correct hours, wages and working conditions. I suggest it is bad for a small group of employees to have their final destiny rest in the hands of a political figure who can tailor these working conditions to suit what he considers to be either budgetary measures or some political purpose. I feel that this outlet should be given to these people in order to draw them more directly into equity with the employees who are not working in the public service of Canada.
During the last session I introduced a similar bill and there was a great leal of discussion on it. It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) participated in the debate, as did a number of other hon. members including the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Creaghan) At that time I do not believe there was much objection to the basic desire of providing the people in the public service of Canada with bargaining rights, but it was felt there was some infringement of the rights of parliament. The bill I introduced last session contained a provision that the report of the

conciliation board established under the act would, in fact, be an arbitration board the decision of which would be final and binding both upon the government and the employees in the public service. The major objection to the measure revolved around the point that parliament was supreme and should remain supreme in its authority to control the expenditures of this nation. Yesterday, of course, we had an example of how this parliamentary authority had deteriorated a little bit when the resolution of the Minister of Finance on tariff matters gave the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) authority to vary taxes without any appeal.
However, the bill introduced during the last session contained a provision that the conciliation board report would be final and binding and objection was taken because it was felt parliament should have the final say in the expenditure of public moneys. Since I felt that the argument had some merit, I altered the bill this year in that respect. Otherwise, this bill is the same as the one introduced last year. When a conciliation board is established, and it completes its hearings and writes its report, that report shall be tabled by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) in the House of Commons either forthwith or, if the house is not sitting, within 10 days after the sittings commence. The House of Commons would be in a position then, in keeping with parliament's right to spend the money, either to accept or reject, amend or do as they liked with this report of the conciliation board.
One other matter was raised last session in connection with this proposal to establish a conciliation board. It was said that the appointment of a conciliation board under the circumstances envisaged in this bill would be weighted in favour of the government because, presumably the Minister of Finance would appoint one member of the board, the union of public service employees would appoint another, and if they could not agree upon a chairman then the Minister of Labour would appoint the chairman. As a result, two members of the board would be government appointees. However, I might say that, in this instance, I wanted to keep as much as possible within the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and I would not want to malign the Minister of Labour in that way by suggesting that he would select a chairman of the conciliation board who would be favourable to the government's point of view.
In any event the report of that conciliation board would eventually be the document tabled in parliament, debated in parliament and decided in parliament, so that parliament would retain its hold on the purse strings of
Industrial Relations
the nation so far as expenditures are concerned, and would also be, by the same token and at the same time, an arbitration board in respect of negotiations among the employees of the public service of Canada and the crown.
The bill is designed to bring justice, equality, fairness and decency into play in the relationships between employees in the federal services and the crown itself, and to assure as much as possible that employees in the public service are not looked upon and treated as second class citizens. The bill is designed to prevent decisions in regard to incomes and working conditions from being made on a political basis, which would continue their existence in a half state of being partly employees and partly not employees.
I feel that the people of Canada, and particularly those employed in the public service, at the time of the passage of the bill of rights looked forward to the day when there would be equality of rights and opportunities. I feel that this bill is designed primarily to bring about just that situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 5, 1960, we had a similar debate in regard to Bill C-9 introduced last year by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). That bill was a little different in form although it had the same title. There was very little opportunity at that time for debate and, unfortunately, we are now in similar circumstances today.
I had the opportunity at that time of speaking for approximately two or three minutes during which time I mentioned that the bill would conflict with section 28 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I am afraid we are faced with the same problem in regard to the bill being discussed today. The hon. member for Skeena mentioned the difficulties in regard to section 28 and I feel that he is correct in his statement. The present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act provides that before a conciliation board can be appointed management-in this case the government-must appoint a member; the employees association must appoint a member and, in the event they cannot agree within a period of five days, the Minister of Labour must appoint a third member as chairman.
Unlike the hon. member for Skeena I cannot assume or believe that such a board recommended by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would be necessarily fair to the civil service association. In order to overcome that difficulty in this bill it will be necessary to add to part II of the act, a new section setting up a board of conciliation specifically designed

Industrial Relations
to consider disputes between employees and the government, as apart from those between employees and private industry. I believe an amendment such as that which I have described should apply in regard to crown corporations as well as to the civil service association because it is possible that wage earners, particularly C.N.R. employees, could find themselves in the same position as do civil servants.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, the government introduced a bill to increase superannuation payments to civil servants. That bill was then referred to a sessional committee of the house. I would suggest that when a similar committee is formed this year the bill now under discussion should be referred to a committee in order that it can be considered by civil service associations and members of parliament.
On March 2, 1961, the Minister of Finance moved first reading to Bill C-71 which is entitled "An act respecting the civil service of Canada". Bill C-71 is a complete revision of the Civil Service Act. I understand it contains a proposal closely related to collective bargaining. I should like to refer hon. members to the March 1 edition of the Ottawa Journal which contains reference to this new step. The main article was written by Richard Jackson, and the opening paragraph is as follows:
An important step in the direction of collective bargaining for Civil servants is being taken in the revised Civil Service Act, the Journal learned today.
The article continues as follows:
This is a concession that staff associations for years have sought and has been included in a brief filed by one of the big civil service organizations with the Glassco Royal Commission on government organization.
In the same newspaper at page 4 there appears an extract from interviews with some of the heads of the civil service asso-cations. Mr. Fred Whitehouse is quoted as follows:
"-if the report is correct, it is certainly a step forward."
Hon. members will realize that Mr. White-house is president of the Civil Service Federation of Canada.
Mr. J. C. Best, president of the Civil Service Association of Canada was also interviewed and is reported as follows:
"If the report is correct I am very happy to learn the government has recognized the weakness in the previous bill".
Because of the length of the session last year, it was impossible to have a further debate on Bill No. C-9. I understand that Bill C-71 provides that the civil service commissioners shall consult with civil service

employees associations with respect to pay and conditions of employment. If this is a provision of the new bill it will mean that meetings will soon take place at the request of the civil service association rather than only at the direction of the minister or the civil service commission. This is a step towards collective bargaining, and I believe it is a welcome one. There seems to be a trend towards collective bargaining for all employees in Canada. Whether or not there will be full collective bargaining in the civil service in the immediate future remains to be seen, but much progress has been made in this direction during the past three years.
The annual report of the civil service commission for the year 1959 shows that during that year there were ten meetings of the advisory committee on pay research. When one realizes that this committee is composed of one of the commissioners and representatives of the staff associations and treasury board, one can see that not only have the Minister of Finance and the civil service commission an opportunity to bring forward recommendations, but this opportunity also exists for the employees.
I do not think the bill introduced by the hon. member for Skeena would be operative, but I wish to state that I am in complete agreement with that part of it which deals with collective bargaining. However, I do not think it would be possible for a conciliation board to solve the problem. Unless the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) extended the provisions of the act, it would be necessary for the conciliation board, when handling a federal employees' wage dispute, to submit a report within 14 days. That would be an impossibility when one realizes that there are approximately 1,900 staff classifications.
If the bill were passed in its present form it would mean that members of parliament would become bargaining agents for the civil service. We would be charged with the responsibility of negotiation in connection with the salaries of the civil service. Clause 1 of the bill provides that this house would have the responsibility, after the report had been submitted, to accept, reject or amend it. This is a complete change from what I understand to be the type of government we have under our constitution.
Hon. members realize that we have an executive and a legislative type of government. If the responsibility rested with the House of Commons, there would be taken away from the executive its responsibility of determining what was a decent wage. I feel that when the sessional committee is set up to review the Civil Service Act introduced on March 2, the subject matter contained in this bill will be fully studied by the committee, and the

staff associations will once again insist upon some sort of collective bargaining.
In conclusion I should like to quote from the magazine Saturday Night of December 5, 1959, which contains an article on the civil service. The article is entitled:
The civil service: Pay it well or cut its numbers.
In that article the author quotes the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) as follows:
"For many years it has been generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service. First the salaries must be enough to do the job, that is to attract enough of the right kind of men and women into the service and keep them in it; second, they must be fair as between civil servants and people outside the service, the taxpayers if you will, which means that the salaries we pay for any class of work should be comparable with those paid by private employers for similar classes of work, taking into account the other terms of employment that are necessary to make a fair comparison."
Mr. Speaker, it is my hope that the civil service commission, the pay research bureau, the advisory committee, treasury board, the staff associations and the members of this house will always recognize those two principles as fair and proper in all wage negotiations.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING TO CROWN AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, I believe the time has come when some sort of collective bargaining for the civil service should be seriously considered. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat referred to the bill introduced yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I secured a copy of this bill from the table, but I think it would be out of order at this time to discuss it. In the first place it would be anticipating debate on second reading and discussion in committee, and in the second place it would raise some doubt as to whether we should be discussing the bill now under consideration.
The civil servant is in a unique position because as an employee of the crown he is actually a part of the crown and is entitled to the many rights and privileges which the crown enjoys, particularly as to salary exemptions. Furthermore, under the Civil Service Act the civil servant has reasonable security of tenure, which people in other branches of the labour force would very much like to have, particularly in this present age of shifting employment opportunities in this country and throughout the North American continent.
On the other hand, I do not think the position of the civil servant is properly understood by the general public. The general public sees him as a person who is sure of his job and salary, and who will be paid regardless of the duties he may have to
Industrial Relations
perform from time to time. Another disadvantage that the civil servant has is that he must take the consequences of policy decisions and must try to carry them out in dealing with the general public.
I think the civil servant suffers more than does any other person from the inefficiency of persons higher up in his particular department. In ordinary commerce and business, if a person is not doing a job satisfactorily he is transferred or dismissed and someone else is put in his place. In the set-up of the civil service at the present time it is most difficult to do this. If you have one person in the chain of command who is inefficient, it brings about inefficiency and dissatisfaction on the part of those who are beneath him in that particular department, and civil servants become disgruntled and discouraged with their position.
In other lines of employment in the commercial world dissatisfaction with pay or working conditions, or with persons who are supervisors, results in strike action if the situation is not remedied. However, by tradition strike action is not taken by civil servants; it is against the policy of the service. In this connection I should like to quote from a leaflet put out by the National Defence Employees Association in connection with this very problem. This magazine was issued in August, 1960, and it contains on page 2 an article by a member of the executive committee saying that the association has assured the government that civil servants will never consider strike action come what may. This puts the association and its employees in a difficult position because they have very little bargaining power when their ability to strike is completely impaired. Yet this embargo on strike action is imposed not by any outside authority but by the voluntary action of the association itself. I should like to quote from the article on page 2:
Let me say this, and I speak as a past president of a union and a member of the CLC, I have opposed strike action by the NDEA and for the following reasons:
We civilians who work for DND in teamwork with servicemen in uniform, have a responsibility to the defence and security of our great nation. We should never forget this.
We have civilians guarding our frontiers alongside service people in technical capacities in remote areas of our land.
We have cipher clerks, typists and mechanics working at alert stations of Navy, Army and Air Force, prepared at a moment's notice to defend our country. Whether they are administration, messing staffs or tradesmen, each by their responsibilities, from the cleaner to the Minister of the Department, are making a contribution to the whole picture of defence.
The enemies of a free and democratic society would be pleased to see a strike against Canada's defensive structure. It could be an invitation.

Industrial Relations
Thus we And that this restriction has been placed on civil servants generally by their own action and by their own association. Therefore, we must consider what outlet these people have when they have a complaint to make in connection with their treatment by their employers.
Regardless of what might be said by various people or organizations, I believe that the government has been most fair in its treatment of its civil servants as to salaries. There are those who would not agree. There are those in categories which did not qualify for an increase who would not agree at all. Yet looking at the over-all picture we find that this government has brought about increases fairly generally across the board. In order to back up this assertion I looked into some figures on the labour force employed by the federal government and the latest information I can find is contained in the December 9 issue of the weekly bulletin put out by the dominion bureau of statistics. I am quoting from the article on page 6 under the heading "Labour".
Federal government employees in September this year numbered 346,084 and their earnings totalled $121,983,000, according to advance DBS figures that will be contained in the September issue of "Federal Government Employment". Excluding staff employed outside Canada by agency and proprietary corporations and other agencies, the total for the month was 337,643 employees versus 342,621 a year earlier and earnings were $118,137,000 against $113,444,000.
I note from the figures that there were fewer employees of the federal government in September, but that they earned more money. The figures indicate an average of $350 in salary per month for government employees. I continue the quotation:
Employees in departmental branches, services and corporations numbered 199,884 in September this year as against 197,743 in the corresponding month last year and had earnings of $67,822,000 versus $60,967,000. Earnings for the half year April 1 to September 30 increased by $23,900,727 to $391,021,388 as compared to a year earlier owing largely to salary increases announced at various dates during this year. Most of the salaried employees in the federal service had received increases by September 30.
Those quotations from the dominion bureau of statistics show, I believe, that reasonable increases have been granted almost across the board to persons in the government services. However, that is not the point at issue. The principle is not whether this government treats its employees well or whether some future government will do so, or whether some past government did so. The point is whether the civil service is to be completely subject to the whim of any government without any opportunity for consultation or any

opportunity of putting forward its view on salaries or working conditions to a body such as an arbitration board.
Yesterday, the Minister of Finance introduced Bill No. C-71 in the house. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I do not think I should discuss that bill but I may, perhaps, mention that there is in it clause 7 which seems to go some way along the line I have indicated. However, that bill will be discussed at some later time and maybe it will be found suitable to the situation. It may be that some amendment will be brought in to make it more suitable, or that other action may be taken by the house and the committees of the house.
In the meantime, to deal with the bill presented by the hon. member, I should like to say that the idea behind it is, in my opinion, to be commended. I think it goes too far in relating the civil service to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and in making civil servants subject to it. I believe that any question of working conditions and salaries ought to come under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. For this reason I think a final decision on the bill before us, Bill No. C-14, should not be made until after the house has had an opportunity of examining and discussing the bill relating to the civil service commission which was introduced yesterday.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING TO CROWN AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
For many years civil servants have been seeking a greater voice in deciding the problems which affect their working conditions and their salaries. The bill which is now before us is a repeater and members of this house who have been here for some years are familiar with its content.
As the last speaker said, I think we all find the purpose of the bill to be commendable in that it would give a greater voice to the civil service in deciding matters which affect them. However, at this stage it would be a little premature to agree entirely with the provisions contained in the bill. In the first place I am not at all impressed with the idea of making use of the House of Commons as a final court of justice in deciding all the problems of civil servants because I think we could have sessions which would last a full year in which the time of the house would be employed doing only that.
If I were to draft a bill according to my own views I would rather stop right there and say that once the report had been made it would be final. In that way there would be at least some finality. There would never be any finality if the report were subject to debate in the House of Commons. I am sure there would be large sectors of the house

that would never want the question to come to a vote or to make their own views known with any finality on some of the problems that would be brought before the house.
I do not agree that the House of Commons should be the final court of judgment as stated in the bill. I do agree, however, that the time has come when there will have to be not only consultation but some provision under which civil servants and the government could agree to have a board or some meeting place where there will be an opportunity to make their representations and to have some finality in the decisions.
I would speak to greater length on this subject were it not for the fact that we have on the order paper Bill No. C-71 which we cannot discuss here today but which I hope in a short while will be considered not only in the house but in a committee. At that time we will have the views of the various civil service organizations in Canada and we will be able to express our own views.
To my friend the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) I say that I agree with the principle of the bill but in view of the fact that we will be discussing Bill No. C-71, perhaps at an early date, there will be ample opportunity then to make known our views and to find out exactly what means the different organizations of civil servants in Canada are able to suggest to remedy a situation which must be corrected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the house has expressed general agreement with the purpose of the bill through previous speakers. I feel that the views expressed by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) come close to what we all think with regard to this matter.
I want to give credit to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for amending his bill this year in an effort to answer some of the criticisms which were made of it last year. I feel, however, that his effort to make these changes has led him into even more trouble. I simply point out the fact that the hon. member has chosen the wrong way in which to deal with this problem.
I disagree with some of the expressions the hon. member used in his opening remarks when he spoke of members of the civil service and their representatives waiting on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) usually with cap in hand and when he used the expressions "inequality in pay schedules result in favouritism" and "the lack of knowledge on the part of some political figure" meaning, of course, the Minister of Finance.
The hon. member knows very well that pay schedules are recommended through the
Industrial Relations
pay research bureau of the civil service commission and that the commission is in charge of setting up classifications and minimum and maximum wages which will apply to each classification and is supposed to be in the position of reviewing these classifications.
Referring to the debate of last year I find that at page 801 of Hansard of February 5, 1960 the hon. member for Skeena used expressions which do not help the cause he is championing. He said, for instance, as reported at that page:
This government In its dealings with its employees, is just about as cheap and chiselling as any private industry I have run into.
He spoke about the employees being treated with scorn and disdain. He described them as second-class citizens. In his remarks today the hon. member said that the civil servants were in second-class positions and were second-class citizens and that their income and working conditions were decided upon by a political figure for whom one can only assume the hon. member has not much respect. That is certainly not the climate in which to present a bill the object of which is felt to be good in its intention. The bill itself, however, is a poor measure.
In dealing with that portion of the bill relating to a conciliation board the hon. member pointed out that the board would be composed of one member nominated by the Minister of Finance and one nominated by the employee association or union. If the nominees could not agree upon a chairman, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would nominate the chairman. As I read the bill the report brought in by this board would be binding upon the employees but not upon the employer.
In his remarks last year the hon. member indicated that the intent of this bill was to cover civil service employees and the employees of crown corporations. As reported at page 801 of Hansard of February 5, 1960 the hon. member said:
If there are rights and principles to be established so that justice will be equitably applied, these rights and principles should apply across the board to all employees whether they work for the Department of Labour under the direction of the Minister of Labour or whether they work for Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines or any of the other crown corporations.
We know that at least the employees of the C.N.R. are served by some of the soundest unions in Canada. As I read this bill the hon. member is now saying to those employees and unions, in effect, "You shall now have compulsory arbitration which will be binding on you, the employees, but which will not be binding on your employers."
I wonder how anyone who claims to have been a union official and who claims to speak on behalf of the unions can put forward a

Industrial Relations
proposition of that nature which takes all rights away from the employees and vests them in a board which, according to the hon. member's statement, in respect of the government nominees would be composed of a member and perhaps a chairman nominated by people on whom the hon. member seems to have no reliance and in whom he has no trust or faith.
The report of that board must be binding on the employees if it is accepted by parliament under the terms of this bill. What if parliament wants to amend the report? What if there were any increases or changes to reduce any benefits that might be given? Parliament could make those changes and those changes would be binding on the employee.
I remember that in the estimates committee we reviewed the workings of the civil service commission. It does seem to me that within the civil service there are many areas where employees have just grievances, and there is no opportunity for them to air their grievances and to bring them out into the open or to get corrective action. I would refer to one instance only and that is in regard to rating cards for civil service employees. There should be uniformity throughout the service, but we find that one department will have a supervisor rate an employee and show the rating to the employee. In another department an employee is rated and he can never see the card, or find out what his superiors said about him. He has no idea what his rating is in that department. There is the right of appeal, of course. But, as we heard, in many instances the right of appeal did not mean very much. In any service as large as the civil service of Canada, you are bound to run into cases of favouritism, bias and discrimination. It is those areas of working conditions which hurt just as much as does the matter of take-home pay.
As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) has pointed out, on March 2, Bill No. C-71 respecting the civil service of Canada was introduced. This is in keeping with the speech from the throne which said that a bill to revise the Civil Service Act would again be submitted to parliament. The bill is now before us. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka indicated, we cannot discuss the details of the bill but it contains provisions which will give us opportunity for a full discussion of how there shall be consultation and meetings between representatives of staff organizations and the civil service commission or such persons as may be appointed by the Minister of Finance to take care of those problems which concern the various service

organizations. When that bill is up for discussion there will be ample opportunity to debate this section and others which have to do with the setting up of pay scales. There will be opportunity for full debate on second reading, and when the bill is referred to the special committee, as the hon. member for Ottawa East said, there will be opportunity for the civil service associations to appear and make their views known. There will be equal opportunity for hon. members to find out what are the facts and then in their judgment to decide how the house should deal with those particular problems. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there is really no particular point in discussing this bill at this time.
I can remember the time a year ago when the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McLennan), other British Columbia members and I met with the joint action committee. There we met with the chairman of that committee, Mr. Stan Stonier, one of the finest civil servants it has been my pleasure to meet. I can truthfully say that when tempers ran highest these were reasonable men who had a spirit of give and take and with whose aspirations I have the fullest sympathy.
I regret that we should be discussing a bill such as this and that the remarks made on its introduction should be so out of keeping with the spirit of the bill. We have a bill before us and we shall have a committee which will give it full consideration. In addition we have a royal commission which is to make recommendations for better operation of the civil service and perhaps within their recommendations many of the points covered by the hon. member will be taken into account.
I move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: May I have an indication from the house leader of what the business will be for next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Monday will be private members' day. On Tuesday we will commence with item No. 11 on today's order paper, which is a resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the tariff board.
The second item on Tuesday is No. 1 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill No. C-47, to amend the Fire Losses Replacement

Account Act. The third and fourth items on Tuesday will be items No. 5 and No. 6 on today's order paper dealing with certain insurance companies acts, and these will be referred to the banking and commerce committee, so I expect that there would not be a prolonged debate on those two items. That is a firm arrangement for Tuesday.
For Wednesday I am not able to be as specific. This is subject to change, but on Wednesday we will likely be considering the Civil Service Act, which in its turn will go to a special committee as it did last year.
Next is the agricultural development resolution which we were dealing with the other day-it is No. 16 on today's order paper-and the income tax bill, which is No. C-73. Members should be prepared for these items next
Business of the House
week, but I will know more definitely on Monday night whether these are the items and, if so, in what order they will come. If we make any progress with the legislation on Tuesday and Wednesday, then on Thursday, either at the beginning of the day or shortly thereafter, we will carry on with the estimates of the Department of Labour, unless the opposition wants to change to something else. We will carry on with these estimates on Friday. In view of the fact that the opposition changed the order of business today, I hope they will not mind if I change the order of business next week.
